Title: How AI–Driven Transformation Reshapes Competitiveness in Incumbent Firms
Source title: AI for Sustainable Digital Transformation: Governance and Innovation
Affiliations: Nebrija University, Spain
Authors with affiliations: Navarro-Meneses F.J., Nebrija University, Spain
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how firms compete, innovate, and coordinate value creation in increasingly complex economic systems. While contemporary discourse remains largely focused on automation and productivity gains, this chapter examines how AI-driven transformation alters the strategic foundations of incumbent organizations. It develops a framework that distinguishes three stages in the evolution of AI capabilities: algorithmic consolidation, anticipatory integration, and architectural transformation. A longitudinal comparative analysis of five multinational incumbents shows how machine learning, digital twins, and simulation platforms reshape decision-making, business models, and stakeholder coordination. The findings suggest that competitive advantage increasingly depends on embedding anticipatory capabilities into organizational governance and value architectures. In doing so, AI-driven transformation enables firms to align innovation, sustainability objectives, and long-term resilience in environments characterized by systemic uncertainty. © 2027 by IGI Global Scientific Publishing. Title: Physics-guided digital-twin-ready surrogate framework for predictive design of double-bridge compliant mechanisms in advanced manufacturing systems
Affiliations: G H Raisoni College of Engineering and Management, Pune, India; Savitribai Phule Pune University, Pune, India; Sinhgad Institute of Technology and Science, Pune, Narhe, India; Government College of Engineering Karad, Satara, India

Abstract: The integration of physics-based modeling and data-driven prediction is creating new opportunities for predictive design, optimization, and the deployment of digital twins in advanced manufacturing systems. In compliant mechanisms, particularly double-bridge configurations used in precision positioning and surface engineering applications, accurate prediction and optimization of amplification ratio remain challenging due to coupled geometric interactions and nonlinear design trade-offs. This study presents a Physics-Guided Digital-Twin-Ready Framework for the predictive design and multi-objective optimization of double-bridge compliant mechanisms. A physics-consistent dataset comprising 8, 000 design samples was generated using Latin Hypercube Sampling, analytical compliance modeling, constraint-based filtering, and response-space stratified sampling. The resulting dataset provides balanced coverage of amplification ratios within the range of 5–50, enabling robust learning across diverse design regimes. Machine-learning models, including Random Forest and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), were developed to predict amplification ratio from geometric and material parameters. The models achieved excellent predictive performance, with coefficients of determination (R2) exceeding 0.99, mean absolute errors below 0.93, and root mean square errors below 0.65. Uncertainty quantification was incorporated through ensemble variance estimation, yielding prediction intervals with less than 5% relative uncertainty in well-sampled regions. SHAP-based explainability and sensitivity analyses revealed that amplification behavior is primarily governed by geometric parameters, particularly beam lengths and flexure thickness, whereas material stiffness has comparatively lower influence. NSGA-II-based multi-objective optimization identified Pareto-optimal solutions that balance amplification ratio and equivalent stiffness, highlighting the inherent trade-off between displacement amplification and structural rigidity. The developed surrogate models enable rapid design exploration, uncertainty assessment, and optimization, while achieving computational speed-ups of approximately 103–107times compared with finite-element-based evaluation workflows, depending on the evaluation method. The primary contribution of this work is the integration of analytical compliance modeling, physics-consistent dataset generation, uncertainty-aware machine learning, explainable artificial intelligence, and multi-objective optimization within a unified predictive framework. The proposed methodology should be interpreted as a digital-twin-ready surrogate architecture rather than a fully implemented digital twin, as real-time sensing, and online model updating are beyond the scope of the present study. Nevertheless, the framework provides a scalable foundation for future integration with experimental measurements, multi-fidelity datasets, and digital-twin-enabled manufacturing environments. Title: Predictive accuracy of the DEB model: forecasting Escherichia coli growth and its uncertainty following substrate shifts

Abstract: Efficient control of industrial bioprocesses requires robust mathematical models capable of predicting microbial dynamics under different environmental conditions. This study evaluates the Dynamic Energy Budget (DEB) theory for predicting Escherichia coli metabolism during sudden transitions between different carbon sources. We focused on assessing the sensitivity and identifiability of model parameters to determine substrate-specific factors and evaluate predictive limits. The DEB model demonstrated high in-sample precision and accuracy. The observed decrease in out-of-sample prediction accuracy was most likely caused by an accumulating systematic error. This error arose from the emergence of unmodeled factors during the final stage of the experiment, which can be mitigated by either preventing these factors experimentally or explicitly incorporating them into the model. Consequently, leveraging its mechanistic foundations derived from mass and energy balances, the DEB model provides application-useful accuracy even with limited data, showing great potential to be utilized as a Soft Sensor within Digital Twin technologies for bioprocess monitoring. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Remote sensing of building height estimation: A review of data, products, methods, and prospects
Source title: Physics and Chemistry of the Earth

Abstract: Building height is a key variable for characterizing three-dimensional urban morphology, vertical development intensity, and spatial exposure, supporting applications in urban climate, air pollution, energy and carbon assessment, disaster risk, population mapping, planning, and digital twins. Remote sensing enables large-scale and updatable height mapping, but most sensors do not directly observe building height. Except for active measurements such as LiDAR, height is generally inferred from indirect cues, including shadows, stereo parallax, SAR scattering, street-view facades, spatial texture, and urban functional priors. Accordingly, remote sensing-based building height estimation should be viewed as a scale-dependent three-dimensional information retrieval problem constrained by observability, observation geometry, reference data, modeling approaches, and application requirements. This review examines data sources, height products, estimation methods, scale effects, uncertainty propagation, applications, and future challenges. We compare passive optical imagery, SAR, LiDAR, and street-view imagery in terms of height cues, applicable scales, and error mechanisms, and review representative products and methods, including geometry- and physics-driven approaches, statistical learning, deep learning, and multisource fusion. Particular attention is given to height definition, product comparability, accuracy assessment, scale transformation, and uncertainty propagation into environmental and socioeconomic applications. We argue that building height products should be evaluated not only by RMSE or MAE, but also by height definition, evaluation unit, reference data, aggregation strategy, uncertainty structure, and intended use. Future research should emphasize application-oriented reliability, standardized validation, cross-city generalization, interpretable modeling, dynamic mapping, and application-adaptive product generation. Abstract: Solar-driven humidification–dehumidification (HDH) desalination is a promising option for producing freshwater on a small to medium scale. It operates at relatively low temperatures and compatible with solar, geothermal, and waste‑heat sources. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning are increasingly being applied to HDH systems to predict performance, model surrogates, and optimize operations and design. Many existing studies use case-specific black-box models trained on limited datasets, without considering robustness, physical consistency, uncertainty quantification, or integration with plant-level control or digital twins. This vision article reviews AI-assisted HDH desalination and classifies applications into two main roles: performance prediction and surrogate modeling, and AI-based optimization of design and operating conditions. Prevailing trends include data-driven estimation of productivity, gain-output ratio, and specific energy consumption, alongside metaheuristic and multi-objective optimization to balance energy efficiency, freshwater cost, and environmental impact. Key research gaps include data scarcity, limited extrapolation to new climates and system configurations, and the underuse of physics-informed and hybrid AI models. This article presents a vision for AI-based solar HDH systems, where AI is integrated from the conceptual design-stage forward. In the proposed framework, physics-informed HDH models are combined with data-driven surrogate models, digital twin technologies, advanced optimization methods, and intelligent control strategies, forming a unified design and real-time operation pathway. © Akadémiai Kiadó Zrt 2026.

Title: Data challenges and metrological approaches in the agrifood supply chain: Data accuracy, data availability, and data privacy issues
Affiliations: Department for Sustainability, Sustainable Agri-Food Systems Division (SSPT-AGROS), Italian National Agency for New Technologies, Energy and Sustainable Economic Development (ENEA), Casaccia Research Centre, Rome, Italy; Premotec GmbH, Winterthur, Switzerland

Abstract: The agrifood supply chain is undergoing a profound digital transformation driven by the adoption of advanced sensing technologies, data analytics, and interconnected information systems. While these innovations create unprecedented opportunities to improve food safety, traceability, authenticity, and sustainability, they also introduce major challenges related to data accuracy, data availability, and data privacy and ethical governance . In this evolving landscape, metrology provides the scientific framework needed to ensure that digital data are reliable, comparable, and fit for decision-making. This review examines the principal data challenges affecting digital agrifood systems and discusses how metrological principles—including traceability, calibration, validation, uncertainty evaluation, and standardised measurement protocols—can be extended beyond traditional laboratory measurements to emerging digital technologies such as IoT, remote sensing, blockchain, Digital Twins, and artificial intelligence. By integrating these principles with FAIR data practices, digital agrifood ecosystems can improve data interoperability, transparency, and long-term reusability while supporting trustworthy data sharing and responsible governance. The review also highlights how research infrastructures such as METROFOOD-RI and governance initiatives such as DRG4FOOD provide complementary examples of implementing these principles in practice by combining metrological rigor with ethical and privacy-aware data governance. Overall, this review proposes a metrological perspective for addressing emerging data challenges and demonstrates how the integration of measurement science, digital technologies, and responsible governance can support trustworthy digital agrifood ecosystems, evidence-based decision-making, and more sustainable and resilient food systems. © 2026 The Authors.

Abstract: The complicated issues that policymakers and researchers face are explored in this chapter, along with new developments and trends in modeling sustainable environmental systems. Integrated frameworks that capture complex interactions among ecological processes, climatic trends, human activity, and policy interventions have replaced isolated domain-specific approaches in environmental system modeling. Multiscale models that successfully connect macro-level environmental changes with micro-level ecological processes have been the focus of recent developments, offering a more thorough comprehension of system behavior across temporal and geographical dimensions. Traditional physics-based models have been combined with artificial intelligence and machine learning to improve predictive skills while controlling computational complexity, particularly when dealing with complicated feedback systems and heterogeneous input sources. By integrating many stakeholder viewpoints into the model-building process, participatory modeling techniques have grown in popularity and have enhanced modeling results and potential for implementation. These cooperative approaches have been successful in bringing disparate interest groups together and converting intricate scientific discoveries into workable policy suggestions. This chapter emphasizes how robust scenario analysis and uncertainty quantification have emerged as crucial elements of contemporary environmental modeling, facilitating more resilient decision-making in the face of socioeconomic shifts and climate variability. Furthermore, new possibilities for adaptive environmental management techniques have been made possible by the development of digital twin technologies and real-time monitoring systems. To improve our ability to navigate complex sustainability challenges, future research directions include developing standardized protocols for model validation across a variety of environmental contexts, refining methods for representing emergent system properties, and developing ethical frameworks that integrate equity considerations into model design. © 2027 selection and editorial matter, Satya Prakash Maurya, Akhilesh Kumar Yadav, Ramesh Singh, Prashant Kumar.

Title: Navigating uncertainty in digital twin ecosystems: A unified framework and key challenges
Affiliations: Faculty of Artificial Intelligence and Engineering, Multimedia University, Persiaran Multimedia, Selangor, Cyberjaya, 63100, Malaysia
Authors with affiliations: Tan A.H., Faculty of Artificial Intelligence and Engineering, Multimedia University, Persiaran Multimedia, Selangor, Cyberjaya, 63100, Malaysia; Chuah T.C., Faculty of Artificial Intelligence and Engineering, Multimedia University, Persiaran Multimedia, Selangor, Cyberjaya, 63100, Malaysia
Abstract: Digital twins have emerged as a transformative paradigm for real-time representation, management, and integration of complex physical systems. Traditional uncertainty classification may be insufficient to address the complexities of uncertainty in digital twin ecosystems. A new class is proposed, referred to as ontological uncertainty, which comprises a novel category arising from the dynamic reconfiguration of the frame of discernment in evolving digital twin ecosystems. A random set representation and an update mechanism are introduced to model this category, enabling both frame reconfiguration and focused exploitation of the current frame. Key systemic drivers shaping the interaction, propagation, and amplification of uncertainties in digital twin ecosystems are determined, with an illustration using an autonomous electric vehicle (AEV) example. A six-layer pyramid framework, constructed from hybrid, adaptive, probabilistic, collaborative, quantum and human-in-the-loop digital twins, is introduced to mitigate uncertainty. A case study is presented using real data on a battery system that represents an important component in an AEV. Significant computational advancements remain necessary to address the challenges of navigating uncertainty in dynamic and complex digital twin ecosystems. © 2026

Abstract: Low Impact Development (LID), such as permeable pavements, mitigates some of the urban runoff effects. Their hydrologic response can be enhanced with real-time forecasting and management. Digital Twins (DT), which integrate physical models with sensor data, offer a solution, yet require methods to handle uncertainties in model inputs and observations. This study presents a DT framework for permeable pavement systems that couples a one-dimensional, explicit-state hydrologic model with a Particle Filter (PF) data assimilation scheme. The framework assimilates real-time underdrain outflow observations to refine model states and provide probabilistic forecasts. Uncertainty characterization revealed that sensor measurement error depends on the underdrain outflow, while rainfall forecast error from the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh model is a function of the magnitude of the rainfall event. The DT framework was evaluated against a baseline model using field data from four permeable pavement types. The data assimilation approach reduced the ensemble forecast error by an average of 20%, as measured by the Continuous Ranked Probability Skill Score (CRPSS), with positive skill scores in 96.2% of forecast events. The deterministic performance of the PF ensemble median, evaluated by Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), also exceeded that of the baseline model. The data assimilation framework yielded more accurate forecasts than a deterministic modeling approach and is computationally efficient for operational deployment. However, outflow forecast accuracy is constrained by the structural limitations of the baseline model, evidenced by poor prediction interval coverage during some high-intensity events, highlighting areas for future model development. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Abstract: Photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting is a foundational capability for operating power systems with high shares of variable renewable generation. However, the methodological landscape is fragmented across physical-based models, statistical time-series approaches, machine learning (ML), and increasingly diverse hybrid and multi-modal pipelines combining SCADA measurements with numerical weather prediction (NWP) and remote-sensing data. This paper provides a unified, practice-oriented synthesis of PV power forecasting methods, linking forecasting tasks and horizons to data requirements, modeling assumptions, and deployment constraints. We first summarize PV plant architecture, the energy conversion chain and key definitional choices (AC vs. DC, power vs. energy, spatial aggregation, sampling interval). We then formulate the forecasting problem across point and probabilistic settings, distinguishing single- and multi-step strategies and showing how horizon choice shifts the balance between persistence, cloud-driven dynamics, and NWP-driven uncertainty. We propose a taxonomy covering (i) physics-based approaches (clear-sky and PV performance models), (ii) statistical and time-series baselines, (iii) ML/DL families — recurrent, convolutional, attention-based, and transformer architectures — and (iv) hybrid and ensemble methods, with attention to calibration and uncertainty quantification. Finally, we identify open challenges limiting robust deployment — non-stationarity, cross-site/climate generalization, probabilistic calibration, and explainability — and highlight emerging trends such as self-supervised learning, foundation models, and digital-twin-inspired forecasting loops. © 2026 Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.

Abstract: This paper presents a software development for the simulation of isolated high-voltage alternating current (HVAC) power cable systems with a digital twin (DT). The DT developed is mainly focused on the estimation of the cable systems behavior over time, concerning primarily the sheath currents and voltages estimation. With this DT operating in a dynamic mode, the behavior of cable systems can be tested, monitored, and optimized. The main function of this DT is as a diagnostic tool for monitored cable systems. In this regard, it is possible to detect faults mainly in grounding systems, when data is available on voltages and currents in the main conductors, currents in the grounding systems, and cable temperatures at specific points. This DT, mainly determines online and in a dynamic mode the induced sheath currents along the cable system. This paper presents the operating principle of this DT and a comprehensive case study, where the DT is applied for monitoring a 45 kV HVAC insulated cable system. With this case study, the functioning of this DT has been shown and validated.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: A comparative review of mathematical optimization techniques for inventory management models covering trends, challenges, and future directions
Affiliations: Department of Mathematics, The ICFAI University, Chhattisgarh, Raipur, India
Authors with affiliations: Nayak P., Department of Mathematics, The ICFAI University, Chhattisgarh, Raipur, India; Sharma A.K., Department of Mathematics, The ICFAI University, Chhattisgarh, Raipur, India
Abstract: Optimization of inventory management continues to play a pivotal role in the efficiency of supply chains, and thus affects profitability, customer satisfaction and competitive positioning. While the surge in sophisticated optimization techniques over the last decade, there has been no comparative review that critically assesses the entire gamut of mathematical optimization techniques (exact, metaheuristic, heuristic, simulation, data-driven, fuzzy, and interval-valued) across deterministic, stochastic, multi-echelon, and fuzzy inventory systems. Our research fills this gap by critically assessing papers published between 2020 and 2025, adopting a systematic review approach based on the best practices in literature surveys. This review’s novelty includes a unified taxonomy linking optimization methods with classes of inventory models, while also considering recent developments in fuzzy and interval-valued optimization, such as volumetric fuzzy systems, pentagonal intuitionistic dense fuzzy numbers, and interval differential equation models, which have received limited attention in previous reviews. Critical insights emerge that: (i) exact methods ensure optimality only for small-scale deterministic inventory models; (ii) recently developed metaheuristic algorithms including the Goat Search Algorithm, Oyster Collection Algorithm, DESGO and the Pelican Optimization Algorithm show better convergence and optimality than legacy algorithms such as GA and PSO for large-scale inventory problems; (iii) fuzzy and interval-valued optimization methods are more effective for modeling demand and cost uncertainties than deterministic or stochastic approaches; and (iv) deep reinforcement learning shows potential adaptability in dynamic environments but suffers from poor reproducibility and interpretability. Shortcomings are noted, including a lack of benchmarking, validation of proposed models for deployment in real settings, and integration of sustainability goals with uncertainty-based optimization. Areas for future development are highlighted, including quantum-optimized inventory, federated learning for privacy-sensitive inventory management, digital twin-enabled inventory management, and neuromorphic computing for real-time supply chain control. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Operational Research Society of India 2026.

Abstract: The rapid and future perspectives on sustainable smart cities’ ever-increasing growth of the global urban population of the 21st century raises the question of how we can transform cities into spaces that not only support the efficiency of urban processes but also resolve urgent sustainability issues. Drawing on a cognitive technology discussion in this chapter, the author explores the possibilities of change in regard to the future of sustainable smart cities. This is because urban management can be enhanced through the incorporation of applications for artificial intelligence (AI), block chain, and digital twin models in decision making and monitoring of urban processes and systems in real time and resource optimization, including offering protection against natural uncertainties such as climate change and natural disasters. The major emerging trend is fundamentally redefining sustainability in the urban context. Self-organized systems of the city, enabled by block chains and distributed ledgers and formally nonhierarchical, provide new possibilities for democratic organization and participation. The exchange of microgrids between neighbors shows that sustainable energy is a way forward economically and environmentally. AI-based circular economy models help improve recycling and reduce waste and, in the process, reduce environmental impacts. The use of computer-generated virtual copies of urban environments as modelling tools helps to predict the problems a city may face and prepare their solution. Moreover, 5G and the advancements of the subsequent generations of connectivity provide the necessary basis for the massive scale of the IoT to provide the fundamental structure for smooth, real-time urban functioning. The set of these technologies enables better management of the demands of modern living by cities, ranging from traffic control to climate change adaptation. Sociocognitive innovations other than technology are constructing options for democratic and engaging urban citizenship experiences. AI-assisted consumer-centric public services driven by data analytics provide relevant services to provide satisfaction and convenience. Rubber stamp intensification of disaster prediction and response clarify the development and solidification of urban intensification, making it possible for cities to be ‘disaster proof’ and be able to recover from a disaster soonest. On the other hand, smart platforms play the role of hubs that bring together stakeholders to share information and make joint decisions in the interest of sustainable development. © 2026 by Nova Science Publishers, Inc.

Title: Agent-based, immune system-inspired supply chain automation for disruption management
Affiliations: Berlin School of Economics and Law, Department of Business Administration, Berlin, 10825, Germany
Authors with affiliations: Ivanov D., Berlin School of Economics and Law, Department of Business Administration, Berlin, 10825, Germany
Abstract: Resilience in supply chains resembles immune system mechanisms in protecting against disruptions and recovery deployment. Addressing a gap in the literature for models that conceptualize supply chain resilience from an immune-system perspective and in response to growing interest in supply chain automation, this article introduces a multi-agent system (MAS) informed by molecular biology and immunology. The proposed models conceptualize supply chain resilience as comprising both preparedness and recovery, analogous to the innate and adaptive components of immune systems. An immune system-inspired mechanism is implemented in the MAS, integrating innate and adaptive responses and incorporating discrete-event and agent-based simulation methods. In a nutshell, the article presents an agentic AI framework combined with supply chain analytics and develops a MAS model readily available for practical applications. The models are developed using AnyLogic software. From a theoretical standpoint, we contribute to resilience theory and its methodological frameworks for uncertainty modeling in supply chains by proposing an agent-based AI environment that replicates immune system mechanisms acting without a priori information about disruptions and so enhancing adaptability to multiple future scenarios. From a practical perspective, the proposed framework and its operationalization in the MAS model supports automated disruption detection, impact assessment, and response coordination through interacting agents that emulate immune-system functions. It can be deployed as part of a supply chain digital twin to assist managers in evaluating recovery alternatives, activating contingency measures, and improving resilience under disruption scenarios. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: A cyber–physical digital twin for secure and optimal operation of smart energy grids under deep uncertainty
Affiliations: University of National and World Economy, Bulgaria
Authors with affiliations: Yordanova Z., University of National and World Economy, Bulgaria; Nozari H., University of National and World Economy, Bulgaria
Abstract: Smart energy networks, as critical cyber-physical infrastructures, face simultaneous challenges such as conflicting operational objectives, data uncertainty, and increasing cyber threats. Decision-making in such environments requires frameworks that can manage system dynamics, information ambiguity, and security risks in an integrated manner. In this study, an innovative decision-making framework is presented that enables adaptive and resilient optimization of energy networks by combining digital twin and fuzzy goal modeling. As an active component, the digital twin dynamically updates the decision-making process and reflects the impact of different cyber-attack scenarios on decisions. The results of various analyses show that the proposed framework is able to significantly improve the quality of decisions, performance stability, and system resilience under uncertain conditions. This study provides a new path for the development of smart and secure decision support systems in the energy sector. © 2026 The Authors

Title: The Decision Twin: Metaverse Patient Digital Twins as Executable Clinical Reality
Source title: Proceedings of the ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
Affiliations: Macquarie University, Sydney, NSW, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Cenacchi F., Macquarie University, Sydney, NSW, Australia; Cao L., Macquarie University, Sydney, NSW, Australia; Richards D., Macquarie University, Sydney, NSW, Australia
Abstract: Clinical AI is no longer bottlenecked only by model performance; it is bottlenecked by the accountable interaction loop through which clinicians and patients inspect evidence, test alternatives, and remain responsible for decisions under uncertainty. We argue that today's digital-twin systems, XR interfaces, and foundation-model copilots each address part of this loop, but they fail when deployed as separate products: predictions are not replayable across time, XR becomes descriptive visualization without executable state, and copilots are fluent without auditable grounding. We introduce the Metaverse Patient Digital Twin (MPDT) as a decision-grade clinical artifact defined by one requirement: every displayed claim or simulated scenario must be traceable to a versioned patient state, explicit assumptions, and replayable interaction logs. We specify minimal acceptance criteria, a reference loop in which stakeholders observe new evidence, update the twin state, run bounded simulations, generate explanations, commit decisions, and then log and monitor outcomes, along with a compact architecture that binds interoperability, simulation, governed interaction, and lifecycle controls. Finally, we outline workflows (risk stratification, diagnosis support, treatment rehearsal, training, cross-site coordination) and the evidence required to make MPDTs defensible: calibration over time, subgroup reliability, category-error prevention (observation vs simulation), and measurable workflow outcomes. © 2026 Owner/Author.

Title: Risk Management in Logistics: Digital Twins and Their Role in Operational Threat Assessment
Source title: EAI/Springer Innovations in Communication and Computing
Affiliations: Wroclaw University of Science and Technology, Wroclaw, Poland
Authors with affiliations: Werbinska-Wojciechowska S., Wroclaw University of Science and Technology, Wroclaw, Poland; Giel R., Wroclaw University of Science and Technology, Wroclaw, Poland; Winiarska K., Wroclaw University of Science and Technology, Wroclaw, Poland
Abstract: Modern logistics systems, integral to global supply chains, face growing complexity and vulnerability to disruptions such as equipment failures, delivery delays, and demand fluctuations. To combat these challenges, digital twins have emerged as essential tools for real-time risk management. This paper explores the role of digital twins in logistics risk management, focusing on operational risk assessment and the application of the Fuzzy Analytical Hierarchy Process method. By leveraging fuzzy logic, Fuzzy AHP enables the prioritization of key digital twin parameters, incorporating expert judgment and uncertainty. The study highlights the benefits of combining digital twins with Fuzzy AHP to improve risk identification, evaluation, and mitigation strategies in dynamic logistics environments. © European Alliance for Innovation 2026.

Title: PCA-OS: A Planetary Climate Adaptation Operating System
Source title: Proceedings of the ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
Affiliations: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore; Alibaba Group, Hangzhou, China
Authors with affiliations: He C., Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore; Zhou X., Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore; Wang D., Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore; Xu H., Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore; Liu W., Alibaba Group, Hangzhou, China; Miao C., Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore
Abstract: Predictive climate machine learning is increasingly good at forecasting hazards, but hazard maps alone do not decide what to do, where, when, for whom, and under which futures. We argue that climate ML remains insufficient for adaptation unless interventions become first-class, versioned, and auditable objects. Many climate digital twins still prioritize state estimation and simulation, whereas adaptation requires intervention observability, counterfactual effect estimation, and constrained portfolio choice. We propose PCA-OS (Planetary Climate Adaptation Operating System), a decision-support operating abstraction built on an intervention-aware global causal knowledge graph. PCA-OS standardizes schemas, versioned updates, query primitives, and audit interfaces across three core objects: (1) an Adaptation Intervention Ledger recording measurable interventions with provenance and uncertainty; (2) a Causal Effect Atlas storing scenario-indexed, spillover-aware estimands, identification assumptions, diagnostics, and sensitivity bounds; and (3) a Robust Portfolio Decision Layer optimizing intervention portfolios under budget, equity, and no-harm constraints. Foundation models and intervention-aware world models should support, not replace, identification-aware causal analysis by surfacing candidate confounders, mechanisms, and spillover pathways for human review. We also outline AdaptBench, an evaluation suite where systems can fail for inequitable or maladaptive recommendations despite high predictive accuracy. The result is a field-level provocation: move climate ML from read-only hazard intelligence to auditable decision support for adaptation. © 2026 Owner/Author.

Title: Disagreement-and-Support Reliability Mapping for Point Cloud Completion in Architecture and Engineering
Source title: Proceedings of the International Conference on Education and Research in Computer Aided Architectural Design in Europe
Affiliations: The University of Osaka, Japan
Authors with affiliations: Hu A., The University of Osaka, Japan; Fukuda T., The University of Osaka, Japan
Abstract: Point cloud completion networks can rapidly densify partial building scans, but their primary risk in architecture and engineering is confident hallucination: geometrically plausible output weakly constrained by measurements, which can silently propagate errors into scan to building information modeling (BIM) workflows, dimensional verification, and digital-twin maintenance. Existing methods provide no spatial reliability estimates, leaving practitioners with an all-or-nothing choice between trusting or discarding AI-generated geometry. This paper introduces disagreement and support reliability mapping (DSRM), a training-free method that computes per-point reliability scores by combining two complementary cues: cross-model disagreement across an ensemble of completion networks with diverse architectures, as a proxy for epistemic uncertainty, and observation support distance from the original scan, as a proxy for extrapolation extent. The fused scores are visualised as a three-class reliability map distinguishing scan-supported regions, reliable completions, and high-risk regions requiring re-scan. Evaluated on 16 self-collected indoor scenes spanning four building types, DSRM achieves a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.827 in detecting large reconstruction errors, with low-reliability regions exhibiting a mean 5.77× higher reconstruction error than high-reliability regions. The method requires no model retraining and adds negligible computational overhead, making it immediately deployable in existing scan-to-BIM and digital-twin workflows. © 2026, Education and research in Computer Aided Architectural Design in Europe. Abstract: The large-scale integration of demand-side resources (DSR) into regional energy internet (REI) presents new challenges for traditional dispatch schemes, including diminishing scheduling patterns, evolving dispatching rules, and uncertain system outcomes. This paper, from a multi-agent intelligence perspective, examines the essence of such complexity and then proposes a digital-twin-based collective intelligence scheduling framework. The framework introduces a holistic cognitive view angle driven by emergent phenomena and leverages the digital twin’s multi-path dynamic simulation capabilities to support proactive dispatch. A hierarchical architecture is developed within the framework, consisting of a system simulator, a situational perceiver, and a decision-maker, which sequentially construct the sample subspace, the feature subspace, and the decision subspace. This structure enables an iterative evolution process that spans the entire cycle, from twin modeling and situational awareness to strategy generation, simulation-based evaluation, and system adaptation. The proposed framework effectively balances the proactive autonomy of DSRs with the system operator's macro-level dispatch capabilities. It overcomes the limitations of purely rule-based collaborative intelligence and fully decentralized swarm intelligence. By integrating collective intelligence mechanisms, emergent cognition, and twin-driven simulation, the framework breaks through traditional reductionist paradigms and establishes a systematic theoretical and methodological foundation for coordinated DSR dispatch in complex systems across multiple spatiotemporal scales and evolutionary paths under uncertainty. © (2026), (Power System Technology Press). Abstract: Salt marshes are climate-relevant blue-carbon ecosystems whose extent, vegetation, hydrology, elevation, biomass and sediment carbon respond to interacting ecological and geomorphic processes. This scoping review synthesizes a frozen inventory of 114 retained records and explicitly separates 23 core empirical salt-/tidal-marsh studies, 26 transferable coastal-wetland studies, and 65 review, contextual and methodological sources. The synthesis shows that optical, hyperspectral, synthetic aperture radar (SAR), LiDAR and uncrewed aerial system (UAS) data are most defensible when treated as complementary sources of spectral, structural and hydrological evidence rather than as direct measurements of total carbon stock. Recent site-specific studies illustrate high performance under particular calibration conditions, but their metrics are not pooled because targets, validation designs, spatial resolutions and study settings differ substantially. Field biomass plots, sediment cores, bulk density, organic carbon, vertical-datum control and independent validation therefore remain essential for accounting-grade blue-carbon estimates. The review further identifies feature-level fusion as a practical default for interpretable multi-sensor modeling, while highlighting the spatial-resolution limits of open Sentinel baselines for narrow and fragmented marshes. Finally, we distinguish demonstrated wetland/coastal digital-twin components from an original salt-marsh digital-twin research agenda proposed here. The agenda links observation-driven state updating, eco-geomorphic models, scenario testing, uncertainty and adaptive management without implying that operational salt-marsh digital twins are already established. Priority needs are stronger tropical and subtropical evidence, reproducible evidence inventories, transferability tests, uncertainty-aware validation and practitioner-ready monitoring workflows. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Digital Value Chain as a Circular Control Architecture
Affiliations: Department of Manufacturing Management, Faculty of Manufacturing Technologies, Technical University of Košice, Bayerova 1, Prešov, Slovakia
Authors with affiliations: Karakai M., Department of Manufacturing Management, Faculty of Manufacturing Technologies, Technical University of Košice, Bayerova 1, Prešov, Slovakia; Bobko D., Department of Manufacturing Management, Faculty of Manufacturing Technologies, Technical University of Košice, Bayerova 1, Prešov, Slovakia; Knapčíková L., Department of Manufacturing Management, Faculty of Manufacturing Technologies, Technical University of Košice, Bayerova 1, Prešov, Slovakia
Abstract: The transition from linear production models to circular manufacturing systems requires more than technological recovery capability; it demands lifecycle-wide governance of information and decision-making. Despite extensive research on Digital Twins and Industry 4.0 technologies, the practical implementation of short-loop circularity – maintenance, repair, and remanufacturing – remains constrained by fragmented lifecycle data and recovery uncertainty. Existing literature largely treats digital technologies as isolated enablers rather than as components of an integrated circular control system. This paper conceptualises the Digital Value Chain (DVC) as a lifecycle-spanning circular control architecture that regulates the transformation of product data into structured circular interventions. Using a conceptual research design based on structured synthesis and abstraction, the study develops a multi-layered framework comprising data acquisition, state estimation, circular intervention, and feedback-to-design layers. Building upon this architecture, hierarchical levels of digital circular enablement – informational, analytical, and decision – are formalised to explain how lifecycle transparency evolves into circular governance. The framework further introduces an operational decision logic structured around feasibility gates that govern maintenance, repair, and remanufacturing pathways. By reframing short-loop circularity as an information-dependent control problem, this research advances digital manufacturing and circular economy theory beyond technology adoption narratives toward systemic lifecycle regulation. The proposed model provides a conceptual foundation for assessing digital-circular maturity in manufacturing systems and offers a structured basis for future empirical validation and simulation-based modelling. © The Author(s) 2026.

Abstract: Spinal deformities, including adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, adult spinal deformity, and early-onset scoliosis, are three-dimensional disorders that may evolve over time through interacting biological, developmental, and biomechanical processes. Although radiography, CT, MRI, and EOS imaging remain central to diagnosis and surgical planning, they provide static anatomical information rather than longitudinal, biomechanical, or intraoperative representations of deformity behaviour. This narrative review examines the transition from static image-based assessment to dynamic intelligence in spinal deformity care. Early AI applications have focused on vertebral segmentation, landmark detection, Cobb angle measurement, Lenke classification, and radiographic workflow automation, but these static models remain limited by annotation variability, domain shift, and a lack of temporal modelling. Emerging longitudinal approaches, including recurrent neural networks, temporal transformers, graph neural networks, and neural ordinary differential equations, may support trajectory-based prediction of deformity progression. Biomechanics-constrained methods, including finite element analysis, physics-informed neural networks, and patient-specific digital twins, may further enable individualised prediction of correction response, implant loading, fixation biomechanics, and junctional risk. Robot-assisted platforms have improved navigation-guided pedicle screw placement, but current systems remain surgeon-directed assistance tools rather than autonomous deformity-correction systems. Dynamic, temporally aware, and biomechanics-constrained intelligence may reshape spinal deformity care, but the maturity of the supporting technologies remains uneven. Static imaging is clinically established, and automated measurement has the strongest evidence among the AI applications reviewed here; longitudinal prediction and patient-specific simulation remain under validation; continuous-time models, closed-loop autonomous correction, and neuromorphic control remain conceptual. Clinical translation will require longitudinal multicentre datasets, temporal validation, uncertainty quantification, explainability, adaptive AI governance, and meaningful surgeon oversight. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Abstract: Hydrogen storage systems operate in a narrow pressure-temperature corridor, hence real installations rarely stay fixed long enough for reliable models. The operating conditions of real-world hydrogen storage systems are changing all the time as tanks age, as weather fluctuates and from other disturbances in the process. Sensor conditions beyond the norm are detected by optimization frameworks using static priors, uncoupled safety limitations, or physics-driven predictions. These limits continually divide the theoretically optimal operating region and the practically safe high-performance region. Present study proposes a novel Bayesian optimization framework that is aware of its environment and can be used with dynamic changes in hydrogen storage environments. A Contextual Sensor-Fusion Prior Builder compresses heterogeneous data streams into a thermodynamically grounded context and generates dynamic priorities to match the plant's instantaneous condition. Using these priors, a Physics-Respecting Contextual Surrogate Auditor validates a surrogate with calibrated uncertainty from physics-model outputs, digital-twin-generated responses, and learned expectations. A Contextual Safety Margin Quantifier estimates the probability of constraint violation more accurately and simplifies multi-constraint safety. The fourth layer, the Adaptive Contextual Safe-Region Explorer, optimizes only safe regions for performance and probabilistic assurances. Cycle-breaking, scenario-driven contextual deployment Emulator stresses-tests generative plant behavior model policy more than 1000 future operating scenarios generated from diverse contextual trajectories. A closely integrated data-driven and physics-respecting ecosystem improves accuracy, uncertainty estimates, and safety under simulated real-world process variability. Our operating policies improve storage efficiency, reduce exploration risk, and create reliable, context-adaptive hydrogen systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Integrating artificial intelligence into nuclear reactor safety: ML-augmented CFD, AI-enabled PSA, and cybersecurity

Abstract: This review provides a structured synthesis of how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping safety-critical analysis in nuclear power plants through three complementary technical domains and cross-cutting enablers. First, we examine machine learning (ML) augmentations to computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and reduced-order thermal–hydraulic models, focusing on boiling and critical heat flux (CHF) closures, interfacial transport, transient emulation, and containment-scale mixing. Particular attention is given to physics-constrained surrogates, verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification (VVUQ), and best-estimate plus uncertainty (BEPU) practices that enable credible acceleration of high-fidelity analyses. Second, we review AI integration within probabilistic safety assessment (PSA), covering Bayesian and hybrid graphical models, dynamic event and fault trees, human reliability analysis enhanced by learning-based support, and digital-twin frameworks that embed online updating of risk metrics. Third, we examine cybersecurity in digital instrumentation and control (I&C) systems, including threat pathways, AI-enabled detection and response, adversarial model robustness, and the coupling of cyber–physical consequences with PSA. These technical strands are complemented by recent developments in uncertainty quantification and resilient AI, together with a dedicated assessment of multi-unit and multi-hazard PSA covering inter-unit and inter-module dependencies, shared structures, systems, components, and recovery resources, multi-unit accident sequences, and single, combined, and cascading external hazards. Across all domains, we consolidate comparative evidence, highlight regulatory and explainability requirements, and identify open challenges linked to data scarcity, plant heterogeneity across small modular reactor (SMR), pressurized water reactor (PWR), and boiling water reactor (BWR) designs, and physics–data integration. The outcome is a consolidated map of methods and datasets, together with a lifecycle governance framework for AI-enabled PSA that links intended use, data and model qualification, PSA integration, configuration control, operational monitoring, requalification, and human oversight to auditable decision gates. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Digital twins and resilience as mediators of climate change adaptation: Evidence from the non-renewable energy supply chain in India

Abstract: Climate change represents a significant challenge for non-renewable energy supply chains. Despite growing attention to climate change, limited research has examined how firms can leverage climate adaptation expenditures to improve supply chain efficiency. In existing literature, adaptation, digital tools, and resilience are often studied independently, with limited attention given to the interconnections among adaptation investments, digital twin technology adoption, and supply chain resilience. The model developed and tested in this study represents a serial mediation model grounded in the resource-based view and resource orchestration theory. The results demonstrate that climate adaptation investments positively influence supply chain management performance both directly and indirectly through digital twin technology adoption and supply chain resilience, including a sequential pathway from adaptation investment to digital twin technology adoption, to resilience, and ultimately to performance. Structural equation modeling was applied to analyze survey data collected from 306 participants in the non-renewable energy industry. The findings of the study indicate that climate change adaptation investments constitute strategic intangible resources, whose benefits are realized when firms develop complementary capabilities in digital twin technology adoption and supply chain resilience. Digital twins can help prioritize, simulate, and optimize adaptation strategies and resilience plans, providing managers with practical guidance for enhancing supply chain adaptability and resilience in the face of increasing climate uncertainty. © The Author(s) 2026. Title: A physics-chemistry-materials-informed neural digital twin for autonomous design, characterization, and optimization of green-synthesized antibacterial silver nanoparticles
Source title: Applied Physics A: Materials Science and Processing
Affiliations: ¹Department of Science, St. Louis Community College, St. Charles, United States; ²Department of Physical Sciences, Jaramogi Oginga Odinga University of Science and Technology, Bondo, Kenya
Authors with affiliations: Agumba J.O., ¹Department of Science, St. Louis Community College, St. Charles, United States, ²Department of Physical Sciences, Jaramogi Oginga Odinga University of Science and Technology, Bondo, Kenya; Okumu F., ²Department of Physical Sciences, Jaramogi Oginga Odinga University of Science and Technology, Bondo, Kenya
Abstract: Green synthesis of silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) offers an environmentally sustainable approach for producing functional nanomaterials, yet optimization of synthesis conditions remains challenging because transport phenomena, reduction chemistry, and nanoparticle growth are strongly coupled. This study presents a Physics-Chemistry-Materials-Informed Neural Digital Twin (PCMINN-DT) that integrates a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) for diffusion-reaction transport, a Chemistry-Informed Neural Network (ChINN) for phytochemical-mediated silver-ion reduction kinetics, and a Materials-Informed Neural Network (MINN) for nanoparticle growth and aggregation within a unified scientific machine-learning framework. The informed neural modules are coupled to a digital twin incorporating Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation, virtual UV-Vis, DLS, XRD, and FTIR characterization, and multi-objective optimization for synthesis design. The framework was developed and evaluated using synthetic physics-consistent datasets to systematically assess its scientific consistency, predictive capability, and digital-twin performance prior to experimental calibration and validation. The results demonstrate that the integrated framework accurately enforces governing physical, chemical, and materials-science constraints while predicting nanoparticle size, aggregation tendency, silver-ion release, reactive oxygen species generation, and antibacterial performance. Monte Carlo analysis indicates robust predictive behavior under simulated process variability, and autonomous optimization identifies synthesis conditions that maximize predicted antibacterial activity and colloidal stability while minimizing aggregation and toxicity. The proposed framework establishes a scalable foundation for AI-guided nanoparticle engineering and provides a pathway toward experimentally calibrated digital twins for sustainable nanomaterials design. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Digital twin-driven zero-shot fault diagnosis of axial piston pumps using fluid-borne noise signals

Abstract: Axial piston pumps are crucial components in fluid power systems, where reliable fault diagnosis is essential for ensuring operational safety and efficiency. Traditional data-driven methods require extensive labeled fault data, which is often impractical to obtain for high-value pumps, while model-based diagnosis is affected by simulation fidelity and parameter uncertainties. To address this limitation, this study develops a calibrated-source zero-shot fault diagnosis framework using fluid-borne noise signals. The source generator is an inverse-transient-analysis-calibrated digital twin derived from our prior fluid-borne-noise modeling work, which uses healthy pressure measurements to synthesize pressure-ripple and outlet-flow-ripple fault signals for classifier training; experimental fault samples are excluded from training and used only for target-domain testing. Directly measured pressure ripples and outlet-flow ripples estimated by a physics-informed neural network are evaluated as separate diagnostic branches in both one-dimensional and synchrosqueezed time–frequency forms. The implemented learning model is a convolutional neural network classifier for zero-shot fault diagnosis of axial piston pumps. Among the tested temporal, residual, and transformer-style backbones, a compact wide-kernel convolutional neural network with a subsequence-length first-layer kernel gives the best one-dimensional pressure-ripple performance. Gradient-weighted class activation mapping visualizations indicate that this kernel scale helps the model focus on complete pressure-ripple events rather than isolated local details. The flow-ripple branch provides a more mechanism-oriented view of leakage-related faults, although its accuracy is limited by virtual-sensing uncertainty. Low-fidelity domain-adaptation comparisons further show that distribution alignment can improve clean-condition performance but degrades under strong noise. Overall, the results indicate that reliable zero-shot pump diagnosis requires synthetic fault data with sufficient source-domain fidelity and a classifier whose receptive field is consistent with fluid-borne-ripple physics. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Abstract: Civil infrastructure assets are managed today through inspection cycles and calendar-based interventions that observe an asset only at discrete instants, so deterioration between visits is inferred rather than measured. Digital Twin (DT) research has addressed parts of this problem, but published frameworks remain confined either to a single lifecycle phase or to a single enabling technology, and few report reproducible validation against public benchmarks. This paper presents a unified DT framework that couples a cyber-physical sensing and communication layer, an entropy-weighted multi-sensor fusion scheme, a hybrid physics-plus-machine-learning surrogate, extended Kalman assimilation for continuous model updating, and a constrained multi-objective optimisation layer that closes the loop from measurement to intervention across all five lifecycle phases of an asset. The contribution is threefold: a phase-invariant state formulation in which design, construction, operation, maintenance and end-of-life are expressed as a single evolving state trajectory; an adaptive physics-to-data blending coefficient calibrated on held-out data rather than fixed a priori; and a reliability-constrained decision layer in which maintenance actions are selected subject to an explicit failure-probability bound. The framework is exercised on a provisional synthetic dataset generated deterministically from a calibrated finite element model of a three-span reinforced concrete girder bridge, and is benchmarked against traditional, IoT-only and AI-only baselines under an identical protocol. All reported results are simulation outcomes; no field validation, laboratory validation or real-time deployment has been performed. The DT configuration attains 96.0% detection accuracy, with a 95% Wilson interval of 95.0 to 96.8, and an area under the curve of 0.98, against 90.0% and 0.92 for the strongest AI-only baseline, every pairwise difference being significant at p below 0.001 after Holm-Bonferroni adjustment. Remaining useful life error falls from 4.80 to 1.30 years, median end-to-end latency from 250 ms to 120 ms, and the annual failure rate from 0.080 to 0.020, raising twenty-year reliability from 0.202 to 0.670 with a discounted break-even at year 5.8. Detection accuracy remains at or above 92% across high-temperature, heavy-load and seismic operating states. A component ablation attributes the margin principally to environmental normalisation at 7.4 percentage points, the physics constraint at 6.0 and continuous assimilation at 4.8, rather than to model capacity, which is held constant against the AI-only baseline. Deployment barriers - interoperability, cybersecurity, cost, power and validation under uncertainty - are quantified and mapped to mitigation measures and residual risk, and a reproducibility statement specifies the dataset generator, splits, hyperparameters, seeds and computing environment, from which every reported figure is exactly reproducible. © 2026 Seventh Sense Research Group®.

Abstract: The study examines the developmental stages of autonomous cyber-physical energy systems (CPES), concentrating on intelligent autonomous grids that incorporate self-stabilizing solar-wind hybrid generation, battery storage, electric vehicles, and AI-driven control mechanisms. A systematic critical review with some features of systematic reviews was carried out at this time. This research offers a thorough examination of the current literature concerning CPES architecture, integrated hybrid renewable and storage systems with electric vehicles, artificial neural networks employed for forecasting and control, digital twin technology, cybersecurity, and procurement trading in prominent indices. This organization employs a relative analysis coding framework that subdivides the study into system layers, optimization scenarios, uncertainty management strategies, implementation techniques, and validation contexts. The study demonstrates that genuine system autonomy is unattainable if isolated component optimization is regarded as the ultimate objective. It has a lot of parts, such as physical infrastructure, sensing and communication networks, predictive analytics and controls, resilience frameworks, and governance structures. HRES-EVS systems are very flexible and can pay off in the long run, but they are hard to use because of unclear policies, inconsistent compatibility with other systems, vulnerability to cyber and physical threats, and a lack of real-world experience that may come from not enough testing. Digital twins, edge computing, the Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence (AI) are all important parts of a flexible closed-loop intelligence system. The paper presents a cohesive conceptual framework that redefines CPES autonomy as an emergent, multi-faceted characteristic of smart energy ecosystems and suggests a future research agenda for the advancement of a resilient, carbon-conscious, decentralized, and governance-integrated Smart Grid. Abstract: The study of the digital twin development as a computer prototype of a water heater is reviewed. The analysis for the uncertain parameter’s presence of water heater mathematical model is carried out. It was found the analytical model of the water heater contains four parameters need to be refine to adapt the model to the real heat transfer process. These parameters include the flow rates and heat transfer coefficients characterizing the heat flow through the heat exchange surface of the equipment. To adapt the water heater model, an algorithm for passive identification of uncertain parameters is considered, minimizing the variation quadratic quality criterion of the mathematical model parameters from the real heat transfer process. Numerical examples showed that the uncertain coefficients identification of the model under consideration belongs to a one-extreme optimization problem. The numerical modeling results have confirmed the effectiveness of the proposed approach to the development of water heater digital twin for industrial enterprises cyber-physical systems. The considered example of developing a digital twin can easily be extended to other types of heat exchangers used in industrial enterprises in heat generation and heat consumption systems. © Pankratova N.D., Golinko I.M., Pankratov V.A., 2024.

Authors: Jiang W.-G.; Wu Z.-K.; Qin Q.-H.
Title: From geometric freedom to value creation: a design-driven perspective on additive manufacturing
Affiliations: Nanchang Hangkong University, Nanchang, China; Shenzhen MSU-BIT University, Shenzhen, China
Authors with affiliations: Jiang W.-G., Nanchang Hangkong University, Nanchang, China; Wu Z.-K., Nanchang Hangkong University, Nanchang, China; Qin Q.-H., Shenzhen MSU-BIT University, Shenzhen, China
Abstract: Additive manufacturing (AM) is commonly interpreted as a geometry-enabling technology. While technically accurate, this perspective underrepresents a more fundamental transformation: the transition from manufacturing-constrained design toward value-driven engineering. In this Perspective, we argue that the central question facing the AM community is no longer “What geometries can be fabricated?” but rather “What value can be created through design?” We propose design-driven additive manufacturing (D2AM) as a paradigm in which design intent, rather than process capability, acts as the primary driver of innovation. A unified three-layer framework integrating functional intent, computational co-design, and cyber-physical execution is established to formalize D2AM. To address the fragmentation of existing evaluation approaches, we introduce the Design Value Index (DVI), a dimensionless metric that captures coupled trade-offs between performance, cost, and sustainability. The proposed D2AM framework and DVI have not yet been systematically validated across application domains; their broader applicability and practical utility therefore require application-specific validation. We further interpret D2AM through three foundational mechanisms: constraint release, coupled co-design, and value-density redistribution. Together, these mechanisms illustrate how AM can reshape the topology of engineering value landscapes rather than merely enabling complex geometries. We argue that AM does not create value directly but can expand or reshape the accessible design space, potentially enabling access to higher-value regions within the performance‑cost‑sustainability landscape. Key challenges, including validation gaps, lack of standardization, and fragmented treatment of coupled trade-offs, are critically examined. We also outline a roadmap toward autonomous, data-driven design ecosystems, including future extensions toward a dynamic and uncertainty-aware DVI using lifecycle data and, where appropriate, digital-twin-supported model updating. This Perspective positions D2AM as a foundational framework for next-generation engineering systems in which design, manufacturing, and lifecycle intelligence are deeply integrated. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Abstract: Conventional cotton (Gossypium spp.) variety development requires 8–12 years - a timeline structurally incompatible with the accelerating urgency of climate-change adaptation, soil salinisation, and textile-industry demands for novel varieties within 3–5 years. Speed breeding (SB) compresses the generation interval by 30–80% through synergistic optimisation of LED spectra, temperature, nutrition, and immature embryo rescue (IER). However, SB alone is a temporal accelerator, not a breeding system: its transformative potential is realised only when it functions as the central engine of a genomics-assisted speed breeding (GASB) platform that integrates molecular marker-assisted selection (MAS), genomic selection (GS), CRISPR and New Genomic Technique (NGT) editing, high-throughput phenotyping (HTP), and AI-assisted decision-support tools. Building on previous reviews of cotton speed breeding and genomics-assisted breeding, the present review provides a mechanistic and implementation-oriented synthesis of these complementary technologies within a unified GASB framework. We evaluate: (i) the molecular architecture of photoperiodic flowering in predominantly Gossypium hirsutum, together with currently available evidence from other Gossypium species where appropriate and its manipulation through LED protocol design and CRISPR targeting of flowering suppressors; (ii) the mechanistic basis of multi-channel LED recipe design from SB 1.0 to SB 3.0; (iii) stage-specific thermal management including the operationally critical 33°C pollen safety ceiling; (iv) nutritional physiology, phytohormones, and biochemical monitoring; (v) in vitro biotechnologies—including callus culture, microspore-derived doubled haploids, and immature embryo rescue (IER)—together with the operational coordination of immature embryo rescue and pollen-stage temperature management within speed-breeding facilities; (vi) high-throughput phenotyping technologies experimentally validated in cotton, encompassing five cotton-specific applications reviewed in a dedicated section; and (vii) AI-assisted phenotyping and digital twin architectures for real-time decision support within the GASB pipeline. Critical analysis identifies allotetraploid genome redundancy, genotype × light environment (G×L) interaction with landrace germplasm, IER scalability, bioinformatics infrastructure gaps, SB-to-field correlation uncertainties, and SVT regulatory requirements as the primary barriers to widespread GASB deployment. A structured 2025–2035 roadmap with three time-horizon priorities and measurable KPIs is presented. Abstract: Industry 4.0 and Industry 5.0 represent two significant stages in the evolution of industrial paradigms. While Industry 4.0 seeks to enhance productivity through technology-driven solutions, Industry 5.0 aims to harmonize technological advancements with social and environmental needs, addressing the growing demand for personalized, ethical, and sustainable production systems. Together, they reflect the dual priorities of technological progress and human well-being in modern industry. © Pankratova N.D., Chernyakova O.P., 2024.

Title: Human–AI Collaborative Neuromorphic Digital Twins with Adaptive Game-Theoretic Intelligence for Fuzzy Multi-Objective Optimization of Multi-Stakeholder Supply Chains
Affiliations: Institute of Economics and Politics, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria; Industrial Business Department, Business Faculty, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria
Authors with affiliations: Nozari H., Institute of Economics and Politics, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria; Yordanova Z., Industrial Business Department, Business Faculty, University of National and World Economy, Sofia, 1700, Bulgaria
Abstract: Multi-stakeholder supply chains require decision mechanisms capable of simultaneously interpreting dynamic system states, coordinating conflicting stakeholder interests, and managing uncertainty across interconnected operational decisions. This study proposes an integrated Human–AI Collaborative Neuromorphic Digital Twin framework in which synchronized supply-chain data are transformed into cognitive representations, enriched through human–AI collaborative intelligence, strategically coordinated through adaptive game-theoretic interactions, and subsequently mapped into a unified decision-knowledge representation for fuzzy multi-objective optimization. The principal innovation lies in this closed and interconnected decision architecture, where the outputs of cognitive, collaborative, and strategic intelligence layers are explicitly fused and transferred to the optimization space rather than being applied as independent analytical modules. The framework jointly optimizes economic, environmental, service, resilience, energy, and operational-risk objectives under fuzzy uncertainty. Evaluation was conducted using combined real and statistically consistent simulated data across six operational scenarios ranging from baseline conditions to a critical scenario involving simultaneous demand growth, capacity restrictions, cost escalation, uncertainty, and stakeholder conflicts. Results demonstrate progressive improvements in decision quality under increasingly complex conditions; in the critical scenario, Human–AI collaboration achieved a 19.6% cost improvement, while the service level reached 99.4%. The findings demonstrate that integrating cognitive representation, collaborative intelligence, strategic adaptation, and fuzzy optimization provides a unified mechanism for adaptive multi-stakeholder supply-chain decision-making. © 2026 by the authors.

Authors: Liu X.; Wang W.; Gao F.; Yuan S.
Title: A Digital Twin Workshop Active Scheduling Method Based on Spatio-Temporal Transformer Prediction
Source title: 2026 International Conference on Unmanned System and Intelligent Technology, USIT 2026
Affiliations: Dalian Neusoft University of Information, School of Software, Dalian, China
Authors with affiliations: Liu X., Dalian Neusoft University of Information, School of Software, Dalian, China; Wang W., Dalian Neusoft University of Information, School of Software, Dalian, China; Gao F., Dalian Neusoft University of Information, School of Software, Dalian, China; Yuan S., Dalian Neusoft University of Information, School of Software, Dalian, China
Abstract: To address scheduling delays caused by dynamic order insertion, processing-time uncertainty, machine abnormality, and load imbalance in intelligent workshops, this paper proposes a digital twin workshop active scheduling method based on spatio-temporal Transformer prediction. The core novelty is a closed-loop mechanism that couples graph-based digital twin state updating, topology-masked spatio-temporal risk prediction, and benefit-cost risk-triggered adjustment, so that schedules are changed only before high-impact risks become critical. First, real-time workshop data are synchronized into a digital twin and represented as a spatio-temporal graph consisting of machines, operations, orders, and buffers. Then, a spatio-temporal Transformer learns structural dependencies among workshop entities and temporal evolution of production states. The model predicts future machine load, queue length, order delay probability, and bottleneck risk. Based on these predictions, candidate schedules are generated and verified through digital twin simulation before execution. Experiments on Brandimarte and Taillard benchmarks with dynamic disturbances show that the proposed method improves risk prediction accuracy, reduces order delay rate, and decreases unnecessary rescheduling compared with dispatching rules, LSTM-based predictive scheduling, and conventional Transformer-based predictive scheduling.  © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Leading-edge erosion is a common form of wind turbine blade deterioration that reduces aerodynamic performance, increases maintenance demands, and shortens turbine service life. Machine-learning-based structural health monitoring systems offer a promising route for detecting erosion severity, but their performance often depends on access to large labeled training datasets. For wind turbine applications, generating these datasets with full-physics simulation can be computationally expensive, motivating the use of surrogate models for efficient data generation. In this work, we evaluate whether a Gaussian process (GP) emulator can replace full-physics simulation as a training-data generator for leading-edge-erosion classification. The surrogate is trained on a limited set of OpenFAST simulations and then used to generate large labeled datasets, essentially cost-free, for a random forest classifier. We apply a parallel partial and zero-censored emulator which extends the standard GP framework by predicting a vector of response statistics associated with aerodynamic, structural, and turbine-level outputs and incorporating output constraints to improve the physical consistency and uncertainty calibration of the predictions. We compare two random forest classifiers: one trained directly on full simulation data and one trained on emulator-generated data. Both classifiers are evaluated on held-out full-physics simulation data across five leading-edge-erosion severity levels. The emulator-trained classifier achieves accuracy comparable to the simulator-trained classifier, demonstrating that the GP surrogate can substantially reduce the cost of training-data generation without sacrificing classification performance. These results suggest that constrained, vector-valued GP emulators can support efficient simulation-based structural health monitoring workflows and may provide a useful component of future digital-twin frameworks for wind turbine maintenance. © 2026 Aidan Gettemy et al.

Title: AetherNet: Bridging Frequency Enhancement and Uncertainty Guided Refinement for Building Extraction
Source title: IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing

Abstract: Building extraction plays an important role in urban planning, digital twin development, and geospatial information updating. Although advances in high-resolution remote sensing imagery and deep learning have substantially improved building extraction performance, structural incompleteness and local misclassification remain common in densely built-up areas, complex backgrounds, and scenes with blurred boundaries. To address these issues, we propose AetherNet, an uncertainty-aware and frequency-enhanced network that jointly models target-relevant structural enhancement and challenging-region refinement. Specifically, a semantic-guided frequency enhancement pyramid is constructed, in which an adaptive spectral fusion module integrates discrete cosine transform -based high-pass partitioning with spatial high-pass approximation to generate multiscale structural candidates. A Pyramid Aggregation Head first aggregates multilevel features to generate a coarse global semantic prior, which is then introduced into a prior-guided spectral calibrator to selectively calibrate local frequency responses and enhance structural consistency. During decoding, an uncertainty-guided iterative decoding block uses the predictive entropy from the previous scale to characterize pixelwise predictive ambiguity and progressively refines deep semantic features and lateral detail features through three-branch spatial modulation and gated fusion. Experiments on three public datasets, namely, WHU Building, Massachusetts Building, and Inria Building, demonstrate that AetherNet achieves leading or competitive results across most region-level metrics and shows consistent advantages in boundary evaluation metrics.  © 2008-2012 IEEE.
