Title: Enhancing X-Ray and Gamma-Ray Detector Calibration via AI-Driven Digital Twins: Predicting Extracorporeal Photon Emission from OpenDose Specific Absorbed Fraction Datasets Using Uncertainty-Aware Transformer Ensembles
Affiliations: Department of Electric and Energy, Vocational School of Technical Sciences, Karamanoglu Mehmetbey University, Karaman, 70200, Turkey; Department of Medical Physics, School of Medicine and Public Health, University of Wisconsin–Madison, Madison, 53705, WI, United States
Authors with affiliations: Bedir M.E., Department of Electric and Energy, Vocational School of Technical Sciences, Karamanoglu Mehmetbey University, Karaman, 70200, Turkey, Department of Medical Physics, School of Medicine and Public Health, University of Wisconsin–Madison, Madison, 53705, WI, United States
Abstract: Patient-specific dosimetry and quantitative external counting for in vivo monitoring of radiopharmaceutical therapies require detector calibration coefficients (k) that are currently obtained through computationally intensive Monte Carlo (MC) simulations. We present a digital-twin framework that learns the mapping from organ-level Specific Absorbed Fractions (SAFs) to clinical k values for X-ray and gamma-ray detectors, trained on 4.47 million SAF entries from the OpenDose collaboration covering the ICRP-110 adult male (AM) and adult female (AF) reference phantoms, 91 photon energies (5–10,000 keV), and 336 source organs. An uncertainty-aware ensemble combining Histogram Gradient Boosting, ExtraTrees, Random Forest, Quantile-HGBT, and a Feature-Tokenizer Transformer (414 K parameters) was stacked via ridge regression and calibrated using Conformalized Quantile Regression. The ensemble achieved a test mean absolute error of 0.220 in log10-SAF space (R2 = 0.921) with an empirical 95% prediction interval coverage of 95.0%. Validation against 10,487 independent published S-values (EMDOSE) yielded a Pearson correlation of 0.990 (log space). The framework reduces k-coefficient computation time from hours of MC simulation to milliseconds, supporting real-time detector calibration for theranostic workflows. © 2026 by the author.

Title: Integrating passive design, renewable energy, thermal flexibility, and intelligent control in net-zero energy buildings: A system-level review
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical Engineering, College of Engineering in Yanbu, Taibah University, Yanbu Al-Bahr, 46421, Saudi Arabia; Department of Mechanical Engineering, Faculty of Engineering at Shoubra, Benha University, Cairo, 11629, Egypt
Authors with affiliations: Refaey H.A., Department of Mechanical Engineering, College of Engineering in Yanbu, Taibah University, Yanbu Al-Bahr, 46421, Saudi Arabia, Department of Mechanical Engineering, Faculty of Engineering at Shoubra, Benha University, Cairo, 11629, Egypt; Alsharif A.M.A., Department of Mechanical Engineering, College of Engineering in Yanbu, Taibah University, Yanbu Al-Bahr, 46421, Saudi Arabia
Abstract: Net-zero energy buildings require coordinated decisions across passive design, active systems, renewable generation, storage, occupants, and control. This article presents a structured evidence map and a focused critical review of these interactions. Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, and ScienceDirect were searched for English-language journal articles and reviews published from January 2015 to 11 August 2026. Database searches returned 4385 query-level records; the imported files contained 4423 occurrences due to a duplicate 38-record Scopus audit subset. Cleaning and cross-database deduplication produced 3180 unique records. Title-and-abstract screening retained 2622 records in a broad evidence map, while 66 sources were selected using predefined relevance criteria to support the focused synthesis. This source set represented the principal evidence types, performance dimensions, and system interactions rather than a statistically representative sample. Evidence was examined across energy performance, indoor environmental quality and well-being, flexibility, resilience, and whole-life carbon and cost. Reported performance depended strongly on climate, building type, occupancy, baseline, system boundary, and control strategy. Passive and hybrid envelope measures reshape building loads, whereas heat pumps, thermal and electrical storage, and predictive control provide operational flexibility. Their effectiveness depends more on coordinated sizing and operation than on individual component efficiency. Field evidence remains less common than simulation and short-term demonstrations, particularly for cyber-physical building systems. The review proposes a performance-oriented co-design and operation framework that integrates contextual conditions, design and control variables, and practical constraints within a coupled building-system model. Research priorities include long-term field validation, semantic interoperability, uncertainty-aware control, occupant-centered operation, resilience assessment, and whole-life evaluation. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Navigating the exploitation–exploration paradox: the impact of industry 4.0 technologies on supply chain performance from the Organisational ambidexterity lens
Affiliations: Department of Operations Management, Newcastle Business School, Northumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne, United Kingdom; School of Business and Law, Central Queensland University, Rockhampton North, Australia; Oxford Brookes Business School, Oxford Brookes University, Oxford, United Kingdom

Abstract: Industry 4.0 (I4.0) technologies have significant potential to improve supply chain performance, yet organisations often struggle to realise these benefits in practice. Drawing on Structural Ambidexterity Theory, this study examines how specific I4.0 technologies affect core supply chain functions, identifies the principal barriers to implementation, and explores how organisational and sectoral characteristics influence implementation success. The study conducted 19 semi-structured interviews with supply chain directors, digital transformation leaders, and I4.0 consultants across the automotive, pharmaceutical, food and beverage, construction, and high-technology manufacturing sectors. Data were analysed using a three-stage thematic coding process (open, axial, and selective coding) anchored in Simsek et al. (2009) partitional ambidexterity framework. The findings reveal that different I4.0 technologies generate distinct impacts across supply chain functions. Base technologies, including IoT, sensors, machine learning-driven forecasting, robotics, and big data analytics, deliver measurable improvements in demand planning, inventory management, manufacturing operations, and logistics through enhanced visibility, automation, and operational efficiency. In contrast, advanced technologies such as AI-driven decision intelligence, digital twins, simulation, and augmented reality offer greater transformative potential but require substantially higher levels of organisational learning, experimentation, and integration capability. The study further identifies five interconnected implementation barriers: process immaturity, legacy system integration challenges, human resistance to change, workforce capability gaps, and investment uncertainty. Organisational culture, leadership commitment, firm size, and sector-specific regulatory and competitive conditions are found to shape the success and pace of I4.0 adoption. Building on these findings, the study argues that I4.0 adoption creates a fundamental socio-technical tension between exploitation and exploration. Structural separation of exploitative and explorative technology initiatives, enabled through cloud computing and big data analytics, emerges as a viable mechanism for managing this tension. The study extends the partitional ambidexterity framework through the concept of Connected Partitioning and introduces Virtual Integration as a digital mechanism linking differentiated capability streams. It further proposes Structural Buffering as a mechanism for protecting explorative technology initiatives from the socio-technical resistance concentrated in that domain, and identifies a sequential ambidexterity pathway in which exploitative stabilisation is a precondition for explorative capability. The research provides a theoretically grounded and empirically rich understanding of I4.0-enabled supply chain transformation and offers actionable guidance for managers navigating digital transformation initiatives. © 2026 The Author(s). Abstract: Intelligent fault diagnosis has achieved high benchmark accuracy, yet performance often deteriorates across machines, operating regimes, sensors, and time. This structured narrative review examines the literature through three connected concerns: the credibility of diagnostic evidence, the suitability and transferability of learning methods, and the assurance needed for industrial use. The reviewed evidence indicates that data leakage, class imbalance, sensor instability, and untested domain shift can make complex models appear more reliable than they are. Traditional machine learning remains valuable when physically meaningful features are stable and labeled data are limited. Deep learning is more suitable for complex raw, sequential, image, or multimodal signals, while transfer learning is useful only when source-target compatibility and negative transfer are evaluated. Explainability can support model checking and maintenance decisions, but explanations also require validation for fidelity, stability, physical plausibility, and usefulness to engineers. The literature further supports a staged route to deployment, progressing from independent validation and shadow operation to advisory use, bounded automation, and gradual fleet integration. Near-term research priorities should strengthen independent validation, uncertainty calibration, efficient edge deployment, and human evaluation. Long-term opportunities include safe lifelong adaptation, reliable fleet-level learning, validated digital twins, and human-centered automation. Overall, trustworthy fault diagnosis should be assessed across the full diagnostic lifecycle rather than inferred from benchmark accuracy alone. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: A Digital Twin and Probabilistic Optimization Framework for Resistance Spot-Welded Joints in Automotive Applications
Source title: Journal of Research and Applications in Mechanical Engineering

Abstract: This study formulates a digital twin–driven probabilistic model to forecast and optimize the tensile behavior of resistance spot-welded (RSW) galvanized steel auto-body joints. Experimental experimentation was performed on multi-spot cross-tension specimens by a Taguchi L27 design with the considerations of welding current (8959–9554 A), sheet thickness (0.19–0.30 mm), electrode force (350–497 N), weld spot number (2–8), and radial distance (12–16 mm). Tensile strength varied from 4.08 Kgf to 150.91 Kgf. A linear regression model accomplished ±5% prediction accuracy in this range, with thickness and number of welds as the most significant parameters, and radial distance as having a significantly negative effect on strength. To offset the weakness of regression, finite element analysis (FEA) was systematically incorporated, allowing for a mechanistic understanding of stress concentrations due to off-center weld placement and to confirm the observed empirical trends. The FEA also showed predictive validity, with calculations at an unseen parameter set (9554 A, 0.27 mm, 350 N, 8 spots) approximating tensile strength to 145.2 Kgf versus the tested 150.9 Kgf (3.7% error). Parameter uncertainty was quantified using Monte Carlo simulations with Latin Hypercube Sampling (170 runs), and Global Sensitivity Analysis indicated sheet thickness and weld radius as overall factors on strength variability. Dynamic tensile testing (1.32–2.00 m/min) validated the model's insensitivity to service-relevant strain rates. Together, the synergy from the combination of regression, FEA, and probabilistic simulations provides a predictive digital twin approach that is both statistically sound and mechanistically interpretable. The approach improves weld performance assessment reliability and provides scalable applicability towards lightweight and safe automotive structures. © 2026, Thai Society of Mechanical Engineers (TSME). Abstract: Background/Objectives: Lymph-node metastasis remains central to staging, prognosis, surveillance, and treatment planning in malignant melanoma. At present, most statistical models assessing nodal metastatic risk in malignant melanoma consider pathological descriptors, inflammatory markers, metabolic alterations, clinical data, and related variables independently of each other. Therefore, we developed a transparent artificial intelligence (AI)-based approach to assess whether the propensity for nodal metastasis is determined by a single layer of local histopathological aggressiveness or by the integration of different biological levels, including local histopathological aggressiveness, systemic inflammatory–metabolic dysregulation, biological heterogeneity, or a clinicobiological pattern. Methods: In this retrospective study, we assessed 73 adult patients undergoing surgical removal of malignant melanoma. The primary endpoint was histopathologically confirmed lymph-node metastasis. Routinely collected patient-related data, including clinical, anatomical, operative, histopathological, nodal, comorbidity, biological, clinical course, and available staging data, were structured into interpretable constructs. These included the Histopathologic Aggressiveness Index (HAI), the Inflammatory–Metabolic Dysregulation Index (IMDI), the Biological–Histological Discordance Score (BHDS), model-estimated nodal metastatic probability, integrated clinicobiological risk, and explanation stability. The AI-based framework was evaluated by applying bias-reduced and penalized logistic regression, machine learning benchmarking, leave-one-out cross-validation, bootstrap estimation, permutation testing, decision curve analysis, rule extraction, feature stability evaluation, network analysis, similarity-based retrieval, conformal uncertainty estimation, and unsupervised phenomapping. Results: For 72 out of 73 patients, nodal histopathology results were available. Among these patients, 22 had positive nodal status. Positive nodal status was associated with a higher Breslow thickness, an increased mitotic rate, ulceration, lymphovascular invasion, a nodular subtype, and palpable adenopathy. The HAI demonstrated the strongest discriminative signal between node-positive and node-negative patients (median values of 67.8 vs. 45.3; p < 0.001) and retained an independent association with nodal metastasis within the bias-reduced logistic model (odds ratio [OR] per 10-point increase: 2.74; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.58–4.75; p < 0.001). The IMDI showed a weak exploratory relationship and did not retain an independent association after adjustment. Similarly, the BHDS did not show significant differences in separating the two endpoint groups. The penalized logistic model including only the HAI showed good performance under leave-one-out cross-validation, with ROC AUC = 0.889, PR-AUC = 0.706, and Brier score = 0.137. Through rule extraction, we found a cohort-specific HAI threshold value > 58.6, above which all node-positive cases were located. With respect to explainability, feature stability, network analysis, similarity retrieval, conformal prediction, and phenomapping, there was convergence toward a dominant high-risk phenotype defined primarily by histopathological criteria. Conclusions: Routine melanoma registries may be transformed into internally evaluated melanoma intelligence frameworks. Histopathologically confirmed lymph-node metastasis among patients with malignant melanoma was organized primarily along an axis of local histopathological aggressiveness, while systemic inflammatory–metabolic dysregulation provided subordinate contextual biological information. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Atomic and mesoscale simulations of silicon anodes in lithium-ion batteries: A review of methodologies and degradation mechanisms

Authors with affiliations: Chen X., School of Aerospace Engineering and Applied Mechanics, Tongji University, Shanghai, 201804, China; Zhao H., School of Aerospace Engineering and Applied Mechanics, Tongji University, Shanghai, 201804, China; Li Y., School of Aerospace Engineering and Applied Mechanics, Tongji University, Shanghai, 201804, China; Liu N., School of Aerospace Engineering and Applied Mechanics, Tongji University, Shanghai, 201804, China; Zhang K., School of Aerospace Engineering and Applied Mechanics, Tongji University, Shanghai, 201804, China
Abstract: Silicon offers high theoretical capacity but undergoes coupled chemical and mechanical degradation, including large volume change, particle and electrode fracture, repeated solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) renewal, and irreversible lithium trapping. This review examines atomic and mesoscale methods used to study these processes, covering density functional theory (DFT), ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD), density-functional tight-binding (DFTB), the embedded-atom method (EAM), the modified embedded-atom method (MEAM), the reactive force field (ReaxFF), and machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs). For each method, we distinguish the quantities it can resolve, its typical spatial and temporal domain, the assumptions that control reliability, and the degradation questions that remain inaccessible. Beyond cataloguing methods, the review links common failure signatures to simulation outputs and experiment-comparable observables, and it explains how validated atomistic quantities may be transferred to particle-, electrode-, and cell-scale models. Emerging directions are assessed conditionally, with emphasis on uncertainty-aware MLIPs, bidirectional simulation-experiment validation, controlled cross-scale coupling, and evidence thresholds for future digital-twin applications. © 2026 Science Press and Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Title: A Simulation-Based Optimization Framework of Stochastic Manufacturing Systems Using External Optimizer
Source title: Journal of Manufacturing and Materials Processing
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, University of Debrecen, Debrecen, 4028, Hungary
Authors with affiliations: Ruzicska G., Department of Mechanical Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, University of Debrecen, Debrecen, 4028, Hungary; Czégé L., Department of Mechanical Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, University of Debrecen, Debrecen, 4028, Hungary
Abstract: In this paper, we investigate a simulation-based optimization framework that implements discrete-event simulation with evolutionary search methods to optimize stochastic manufacturing systems efficiently. The proposed methodology couples a Tecnomatix Plant Simulation model with a MATLAB R2025b-based optimization environment using a data exchange interface, allowing for the iterative assessment of complex manufacturing systems. The study examines an adaptive replication strategy designed to manage stochastic variability in simulation outcomes. In the proposed method, the required number of simulation runs are determined dynamically based on confidence interval estimation. The stopping criterion is specified using a 95% confidence interval, ensuring adequate statistical accuracy while decreasing excess computational effort. The framework allows multiple performance indicators, such as throughput, congestion levels, and machine failures, which are built into an objective function. The optimization is driven by a (1, λ)-evolution strategy with Gaussian mutation and adaptive step-size control, allowing robust search in noisy objective function. However, thanks to the framework presented, it is also possible to apply other optimization algorithms. A case study of a manufacturing system was built and modeled in Tecnomatix Plant Simulation to validate the proposed methodology. In comparison with the baseline production configuration in one of the simulation runs, the suggested framework reduced the objective function by 43.36%. Benchmark experiments demonstrated that the adaptive replication strategy achieved a solution quality comparable to fixed replication schemes while requiring fewer simulation evaluations on average, thereby reducing the computational effort without compromising statistical reliability. The benchmark comparison showed that the adaptive replication strategy improved the objective value by up to 17.20% compared with fixed-replication strategies while requiring substantially less computational time than the fixed-20 and fixed-30 strategies. The robustness analysis further demonstrates that the adaptive replication strategy produces consistent optimization results across independent runs despite the stochastic nature of both the simulation model and the optimization process. From an industrial perspective, the proposed framework provides a practical decision-support tool for the optimization of manufacturing systems under uncertainty, enabling more reliable parameter tuning with reduced computational effort and facilitating the implementation of digital twin technologies. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: IoT-Enabled Impedance-Aware Edge Intelligence for Control-Structure Inversion and Multiscale Parameter Identification of Grid-Forming Energy Storage Systems
Affiliations: Xinjiang University, School of Electrical Engineering, Urumqi, 830046, China; State Grid Xinjiang Electric Power Co., Ltd, Electric Power Research Institute, Urumqi, 830001, China; North China Electric Power University, School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Beijing, 102206, China

Abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) monitoring in grid-forming (GFM) energy-storage plants exposes multi-rate terminal measurements but rarely the proprietary controller topology, internal states, or gains required by an edge-to-cloud digital twin. We present impedance-conditioned control-structure inversion and sequential parameter identification (ICI-SPI), an IoT-enabled, physics-guided framework that separates structural ambiguity from weak parameter observability. Native-rate waveform tokens are fused with complex dq-impedance evidence; a typed graph decoder then proposes executable controller graphs, which are rejected unless they reproduce both impedance and transient behavior while satisfying structural constraints. A generalized virtual-impedance observer reconstructs hidden electromotive-force states before slow outer-loop and fast inner-loop parameters are fitted in sequence. An observability gate returns a point estimate only when data-Jacobian rank, information, correlation, and uncertainty tests pass; otherwise it reports an interval or a graph-equivalence set. Distillation, integer-8 quantization, and event-triggered synchronization provide an edge-compatible path without conflating local inference cost with communication savings. Controlled electromagnetic-transient (EMT) experiments across virtual-synchronous-machine, droop, matching, and dispatchable-virtual-oscillator controllers yield 96.1% macro-F1, 0.36 typed graph edit distance, and 2.8% impedance normalized root-mean-square error. Selective parameter mean absolute percentage error is 3.2% at 91.3% point-estimate availability. The quantized student retains 95.4% macro-F1 and sends 31% of full digital-twin update packets. These results support structure-first IoT intelligence within the tested controller library and operating envelope. © 2014 IEEE.

Title: Carbon offset-aware economic scheduling using echo state enhanced variational mode decomposition and ARIMA forecasting for P2X-based city energy ecosystems with joint green-carbon certificate and socio-financial welfare

Authors with affiliations: Zhou J., Yancheng Teathers University, Jiangsu, Yancheng, 224002, China; Chen Y., School of Management Engineering and Business, Hebei University of Engineering, Hebei, Handan, 056038, China
Abstract: Urban energy systems in sustainable cities are facing increasing challenges due to the simultaneous integration of hydrogen-based conversion, carbon regulation, renewable energy uncertainty, and emerging electric mobility demands. This paper develops a low-carbon optimization framework for a Multi-Energy Distribution Network that coordinates electricity, gas, heat, and hydrogen infrastructures while incorporating Power-to-X technologies, hydrogen-enriched gas utilization, carbon capture, and aerial electric mobility. The proposed framework integrates ADTAN-driven Electric Taxi Drone demand modeling, Digital Twin synchronization, Blockchain-based trusted coordination, ARIMA-based source-load forecasting, and a hybrid Stackelberg Game, Mechanism Design, and Nash Game structure within a unified scheduling framework. A mixed-integer optimization model is formulated considering green certificate trading, ladder-type carbon trading, and socio-financial welfare to achieve coordinated multi-energy management. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is evaluated through a large-scale urban energy system case study. Numerical results demonstrate that coordinated hydrogen blending and environmental market mechanisms reduce operating costs by 25.2% and carbon emissions by 17.2% compared with the baseline case. Moreover, wind power utilization increases from 71.5% to 98.8%, while renewable curtailment penalties decrease by more than 95%. The integrated Digital Twin and Blockchain layers further enhance operational transparency, synchronization capability, and coordination reliability, supporting the development of resilient and low-carbon urban energy management strategies. © 2026 The Authors

Abstract: Rhythm control therapy has an important role in atrial fibrillation (AF) management, and antiarrhythmic drugs (AADs) remain essential for pharmacological cardioversion, maintenance of sinus rhythm, reduction in AF burden, and treatment before or after catheter ablation. However, their efficacy varies substantially among patients, while proarrhythmia, organ toxicity, drug interactions, and treatment discontinuation frequently limit their use. Current drug selection therefore relies mainly on safety-based exclusion based on structural heart disease, ventricular function, coronary disease, renal or hepatic function, and baseline conduction and repolarization characteristics, rather than on individualized prediction of comparative therapeutic benefit. This narrative review examines the potential role of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), computational electrophysiology, and cardiac digital twins across the AAD treatment pathway. Particular attention is given to patient selection, comparative drug choice, prediction of cardioversion success and sinus-rhythm maintenance, dose optimization, proarrhythmia assessment, extracardiac toxicity, and longitudinal safety surveillance. AI can potentially integrate clinical, electrocardiographic (ECG), imaging, wearable, genomic, and pharmacological data to estimate patient-specific efficacy and toxicity. ML models have already demonstrated the feasibility of predicting drug-induced QT prolongation from electronic health records and detecting ECG signatures associated with drug-induced arrhythmic risk. Moreover, patient-specific AF digital twins have been used to simulate electrophysiological responses to amiodarone and identify patients with different subsequent rhythm outcomes. Nevertheless, most available applications remain retrospective, single-center, non-comparative, or proof-of-concept, and few directly support selection among alternative AADs. Most are prognostic, estimate outcomes under observed care, or predict drug-specific toxicity; models that estimate outcomes under alternative AADs remain the essential missing element. AI-supported antiarrhythmic therapy represents a promising transition from population-based prescribing toward individualized estimation of efficacy, toxicity, and monitoring requirements. Its clinical adoption will require multicenter external validation, causal treatment-effect modeling, prospective workflow evaluation, randomized impact trials, transparent uncertainty reporting, and continued clinician oversight. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Digital Twin in Vehicular Communications: Challenges and Opportunities

Abstract: Digital twins (DTs) are increasingly studied together with vehicular communications, but the literature spans different twinned entities, synchronization assumptions, computing placements, and levels of experimental evidence, which makes results difficult to compare. This survey provides a communication-centric review of DT-enabled vehicular systems. We first introduce an operational definition for a vehicular DT and distinguish a synchronized DT from a static simulator or digital model. We then organize the field according to twin granularity, physical–virtual synchronization, vehicle–edge–cloud placement, enabling V2X technologies, and measurable evaluation dimensions. The standardization discussion is updated from DSRC and IEEE 802.11p through 5G-Advanced and ongoing 3GPP work toward 6G, together with recent digital-twin and network-digital-twin standards. Rather than treating reported benefits as established outcomes, we compare the assumptions, metrics, evidence, limitations, deployment constraints, and safety and security implications of representative studies. Finally, we identify research priorities involving synchronization staleness, twin placement and migration, communication–computation–fidelity tradeoffs, validation and uncertainty, interoperable data models, lifecycle management, and safety-aware closed-loop operation. The survey is intended to provide researchers and practitioners with a structured basis for deciding when DT techniques are appropriate for vehicular communication systems and how such systems should be evaluated. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Digital Twins for Sustainable Groundwater Resources Management: From Monitoring and Prediction to Governance and Resilience—A Review
Affiliations: Department of Mathematics, Computer Sciences, Physics and Earth Sciences, The University of Messina, Messina, 98166, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Borzì I., Department of Mathematics, Computer Sciences, Physics and Earth Sciences, The University of Messina, Messina, 98166, Italy
Abstract: This article presents a scoping review of the literature on digital twins (DTs) for sustainable groundwater resources management, which constitutes a very recent and rapidly expanding research field, with literature moving quickly from conceptual frameworks to application-oriented systems. The literature, selected through the PRISMA 2020 methodology, is organized into seven sub-topics: AI and ML foundations, digital twin architectures and frameworks, aquifer-scale DT applications, agricultural and water–energy–food (WEF) nexus DTs, basin and urban water DTs, sensing, monitoring and IoT infrastructures, and governance, resilience and socio-hydrology. This structure shows how the field is shifting from monitoring and prediction toward integrated decision support, where process-based models, machine learning surrogates, real-time sensing and optimization are combined to support drought mitigation, saltwater intrusion control, irrigation management, climate adaptation and basin-scale planning. Across the reviewed studies, the most recurrent contributions are the construction of hybrid model architectures, the use of DTs to close the loop between observation and control, and the growing recognition that groundwater management must incorporate governance, stakeholder decision-making and socio-hydrological feedbacks. At the same time, the literature still faces key limitations, especially uncertainty quantification, interoperability between models and data streams, transferability to data-scarce settings and limited validation under real operational conditions. Future research should therefore focus on physics-informed and explainable AI, federated and scalable DT architectures, stronger coupling with socio-hydrological and governance frameworks, and more field-tested implementations that can demonstrate robust performance across diverse hydrogeological and institutional contexts. © 2026 by the author.

Title: Digital twin-driven deep learning and multi-agent reinforcement learning for energy management of smart microgrids

Abstract: The increasing integration of electric vehicles (EVs) and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology introduces significant operational challenges in modern power systems, mainly due to the high uncertainty of renewable generation and rapidly varying demand profiles. Conventional energy management approaches are often based on simplified system models or centralized optimization schemes, which struggle to capture system dynamics in real time and scale effectively under highly stochastic and large-scale operating conditions. This paper proposes a unified framework that can simultaneously provide accurate prediction of uncertain resources, real-time system representation, and adaptive decentralized decision-making for large-scale EV coordination. In this regard, this paper proposes an integrated framework combining Digital Twin Technology (DTT), Deep Neural Networks (DNN), and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) for real-time EV charging and discharging optimization. This integration enables coordinated prediction, decision support, and distributed control within a data-driven framework, improving adaptability compared to conventional standalone approaches. Within this framework, EVs are dynamically adapted with uncertain resources enabling efficient local energy management in which a 22.3% reduction in operational cost and a 38% decrement in battery aging, compared to the Intelligent Battery Life Enhancement Method is achieved © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Applications of reactor produced radioisotopes for radioactive particle tracking (RPT) studies in various multiphase process columns

Abstract: Multiphase process columns, including fluidized beds, risers and downers, bubble columns, slurry and trickle-bed reactors, and three-phase contactors, are widely used in catalytic cracking, combustion, gasification, and chemical synthesis. Their internal hydrodynamics remain difficult to characterize because these systems are opaque, densely loaded, and often operate under harsh conditions. Radioactive particle tracking (RPT) overcomes these limitations by tracking the three-dimensional Lagrangian motion of a gamma-emitting tracer particle using an external array of scintillation detectors, enabling non-invasive measurement of particle trajectories, velocity fields, residence-time distributions, dispersion coefficients, granular temperature, and mixing characteristics. This review covers reactor-produced radioisotopes, including production routes, nuclear and physical characteristics (gamma energy, emission yield, half-life, chemical compatibility), isotope-selection criteria, and tracer/particle preparation, along with the radioisotope-RPT linkage that remains under addressed despite being fundamental to measurement accuracy. It then details RPT methodology, including detector systems, particle-localization and trajectory-reconstruction algorithms, and the hydrodynamic parameters derivable from tracked trajectories, such as velocity and turbulence statistics, solids/liquid holdup, circulation patterns, dispersion coefficients, and residence-time distributions, along with sources of uncertainty. Applications across gas–solid, gas–liquid, liquid–solid, and gas–liquid-solid columns are synthesized to compare reactor configurations, identify hydrodynamic consensus and contradictions, and examine RPT's role in validating CFD/DEM models against complementary diagnostics such as PEPT, gamma-ray CT, and gamma-scanning densitometry. Current limitations in detector calibration and isotope logistics are discussed alongside emerging opportunities in machine-learning-assisted reconstruction and digital-twin integration. © Akadémiai Kiadó Zrt 2026.

Title: Smart technology and multibody simulation for skier safety: a structured narrative review and research roadmap
Source title: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living

Abstract: This structured narrative review examines how smart equipment, wearable and environmental sensing, digital twins, and multibody simulation can contribute to skier safety and prevention of ski-injury. The Scopus® search produced 58, 919 aggregate query returns; after excluding two deliberately broad searches, 1, 285 targeted-query records were screened and 74 sources were retained. The backward and the forward search for citation searches supported by Google Scholar™ identified another 76 sources, giving 150 included sources. Because the literature is heterogeneous in study design, outcome, and technological maturity, the evidence was synthesised qualitatively rather than by meta-analysis. The review distinguishes technologies that are already useful for measurement or protection from approaches that remain experimental or conceptual. It also identifies validation, calibration, uncertainty quantification, interoperability, false-alarm control, and field robustness as the principal barriers to real-time predictive safety systems. Finally, a non-validated Human–Skills–Equipment–Environment framework and a conceptual Skier Safety Index are presented solely as hypotheses for future research. The resulting roadmap prioritises prospective validation with human-subject data, standardised multimodal data sets, transparent model verification, and controlled evaluation of adaptive safety interventions. © 2026 Muscolo and Binosi.

Abstract: The rapid expansion of grid-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) is reshaping modern power systems under increasing renewable penetration. As storage simultaneously supports energy arbitrage, ancillary services, peak shaving, and renewable integration, conventional model-based optimization faces growing challenges in scalability and uncertainty. Artificial intelligence (AI), including deep learning, reinforcement learning, graph neural networks, federated learning, and large language models (LLMs), has emerged as a powerful tool for storage optimization. This review organizes recent advances into three areas: state perception, dispatch and scheduling, and capacity planning. Across these applications, AI has demonstrated substantial improvements in operational performance and planning efficiency, although results remain highly dependent on market conditions and system characteristics. Key challenges - including interpretability, safety, sim-to-real transfer, and cybersecurity - suggest that AI should complement rather than replace physics-based optimization. We conclude by highlighting future research directions in optimality, safety, and scalable deployment. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Intelligent Transportation Systems: A Review of Integration of Digital Twin and Machine Learning Control
Affiliations: School of Engineering, Computer and Mathematical Sciences, Auckland University of Technology, 6-24 St. Paul Street, Auckland, 1010, New Zealand
Authors with affiliations: Tun T., School of Engineering, Computer and Mathematical Sciences, Auckland University of Technology, 6-24 St. Paul Street, Auckland, 1010, New Zealand; Sabit H., School of Engineering, Computer and Mathematical Sciences, Auckland University of Technology, 6-24 St. Paul Street, Auckland, 1010, New Zealand
Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive review of the integration of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) and Digital Twin (DT) technologies for intelligent traffic management. It examines the role of key enabling technologies, including the Internet of Things (IoT), machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), reinforcement learning (RL), Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication, and edge computing. These technologies support real-time traffic monitoring, traffic prediction, and adaptive control in ITS. The review synthesizes recent research on conventional traffic control methods, optimization-based approaches, learning-based techniques, and DT-enabled traffic management solutions. Particular attention is given to the integration of DTs with intelligent traffic signal control, real-time synchronization, multi-intersection coordination, communication latency, sensing uncertainty, and scalability. The reviewed literature demonstrates the potential of DT-enabled ITS to improve traffic efficiency, reduce congestion, enhance transportation safety, and support sustainable mobility through data-driven decision-making. However, significant challenges remain regarding communication delays, sensor and data uncertainty, computational complexity, scalability, and validation under realistic urban conditions. Based on the reviewed literature, this paper identifies key research gaps and outlines future research directions toward scalable, reliable, adaptive, and real-time DT-enabled ITS architectures for next-generation smart cities. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: Solar thermal calorimeters serve as foundational reference instruments for quantifying absorbed thermal power, evaluating optical-to-thermal conversion efficiency, and validating computational models in concentrated solar thermal (CST) research. This review synthesizes recent numerical, thermo-hydraulic, and experimental advancements, evaluating the evolution from basic single-tube configurations to high-confinement cavity calorimeters (achieving apparent absorptances (Formula presented.)) and flat-plate architecture enhanced with impinging jets and internal fin arrays. The selection of working fluids is examined; water accounts for approximately (Formula presented.) of reported implementations due to low property uncertainty, whereas synthetic oils and gaseous coolants expand operating temperature ranges at the expense of thermochemical degradation and parasitic pumping penalties. Furthermore, critical thermo-hydraulic challenges induced by extreme non-uniform heat fluxes are identified, including structural thermal bowing, parallel-channel flow maldistribution, recirculation traps, and buoyancy-driven instabilities occurring at Richardson numbers (Formula presented.). Metrological constraints related to solar reflection interference in non-contact thermometry and calibration drift in photometric target arrays are also critically addressed. Finally, key strategic research directions are outlined, emphasizing high-temperature advanced materials, active flow equalization, real-time multi-physics digital twins, and standardized dynamic testing metrology. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Information-Theoretic Path Planning for Safe and Adaptive Nanobot Drug Delivery
Affiliations: Engineering Management and Systems Engineering, Old Dominion University, Norfolk, VA, United States; Macon and Joan Brock Virginia Health Sciences, Old Dominion University, Norfolk, VA, United States; Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Old Dominion University, Norfolk, VA, United States

Abstract: We present a safe and efficient path planning framework for nanobot navigation in complex vascular networks, enabling precise drug delivery to hard-to-reach tumor regions such as those found in the lungs. The proposed method introduces a safe and efficient path planning strategy that integrates a utility-based function to balance two key goals: exploring uncertain areas to gather valuable information and avoiding hazardous regions to ensure safe and reliable delivery. We evaluate a simplified swarm-based nanobot navigation scenario using synthetic vascular maps that mimic the structural complexity of lung tumor blood vessels. Environmental uncertainty is modeled from vessel topology, blockage density, and flow dynamics to simulate real biological conditions. Each navigation trial is evaluated based on how well the nanobot avoids risky regions, reduces environmental uncertainty, and reaches the target efficiently. Our methodology builds on established literature in information-theoretic (IT) planning and biomedical robotics. Compared with the classical rapidly exploring random tree star (RRT∗) baseline, the proposed RRT∗-IT approach achieved 79% greater information gain (IG, 8.06 vs. 4.50, computed via Bayesian entropy updating) while reducing the navigational risk (NR) rate from 40.0% to 22.9%, resulting in safer trajectories in high-complexity vascular networks. Planning times averaging 1.05 ± 0.18 s per run, confirming computational feasibility for offline preoperative planning in biomedical applications. The modular design is scalable and ready to integrate future extensions, such as real-time sensor feedback, digital twin models, and patient-specific anatomy. This work contributes a validated planning algorithm that improves delivery safety and reliability by guiding nanobots away from high-risk zones and toward clinically relevant targets. It serves as a validated computational baseline for future development of intelligent, uncertainty-aware microrobotic platforms. Copyright © 2026 Nagesh Bheesetty et al. Title: Auditing digital-twin acceleration measurements for synthetic-to-real induction motor fault diagnosis
Affiliations: School of Automation, Qingdao University, Qingdao, China
Authors with affiliations: Zhao T., School of Automation, Qingdao University, Qingdao, China; Ji Z., School of Automation, Qingdao University, Qingdao, China
Abstract: Digital twins can generate labelled motor-fault signals without repeatedly reproducing faults on physical machines, but synthetic measurements may not match real sensor behaviour closely enough for diagnostic transfer. The purpose of this offline study of bench-test data is to determine whether and to what extent digital-twin acceleration measurements can support fault classification of real bench-test measurements when no or only a few real calibration windows are available. The common acceleration channels of the real UOEMD-VAFCVS and synthetic DT-UOIMSD datasets are analysed with a balanced-clean protocol that excludes a documented digital-twin grid anomaly, keeps every acquisition file in one split role, and evaluates file-level predictions. The analysis audits fidelity by label, channel, amplitude, and frequency, and evaluates zero-shot transfer, paired few-shot calibration over seven real adaptation condition cells and five seeds, target-only baselines, and probability calibration. Zero-shot transfer is weak, with macro-F1 0.087 [0.084, 0.090] and expected calibration error (ECE) 0.738 [0.732, 0.744]. With five overlapping support windows per class from one real adaptation acquisition, the selected source-plus-support weighted method reaches macro- (Formula presented) (Formula presented) 1 0.234 [0.190, 0.279], balanced accuracy 0.267 [0.226, 0.306], and ECE 0.568 [0.528, 0.608], where the intervals use condition-cell cluster bootstrap. Its gain over the strongest target-only baseline is small and condition-dependent. These findings support a bench-based, pre-deployment audit; they do not establish online operational diagnostic performance or justify replacing real measurements. © 2026 IOP Publishing Ltd. Title: The Role of Digital Twins in Improving River Water Quality
Affiliations: Tata Consultancy Services Research, Tata Consultancy Services, Maharashtra, Pune, India
Authors with affiliations: Barat S., Tata Consultancy Services Research, Tata Consultancy Services, Maharashtra, Pune, India; Kausley S., Tata Consultancy Services Research, Tata Consultancy Services, Maharashtra, Pune, India; Thakur P.S., Tata Consultancy Services Research, Tata Consultancy Services, Maharashtra, Pune, India; Shrivastava S., Tata Consultancy Services Research, Tata Consultancy Services, Maharashtra, Pune, India; Kulkarni V., Tata Consultancy Services Research, Tata Consultancy Services, Maharashtra, Pune, India; Rai B., Tata Consultancy Services Research, Tata Consultancy Services, Maharashtra, Pune, India
Abstract: Rivers act as primary sources for drinking water, irrigation, industrial use, and habitats for aquatic life. The degradation of river water quality, therefore, not only adversely affects public health but also disrupts aquatic ecosystems, leading to biodiversity loss and impacting communities that rely on rivers for food and income. As a result, ensuring river water quality is a critical need and a significant challenge that calls for precise understanding of several related aspects affecting water quality as well as the dynamics of water flow, such as river characteristics, environmental elements, human-induced activities, riverbed and its self-healing capacity, hydraulic flows, atmospheric influences, and anthropogenic elements like industrial discharges and agricultural runoff. Current monitoring methods rely on sensing water quality parameters such as pH levels, dissolved oxygen (DO), biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), and chemical oxygen demand (COD) at specific points and times. This leads to point solutions that are valid for limited timeframes, where the need is to have a holistic solution for the entire river over a longer period of time. This chapter examines the multifaceted river water quality dynamics by considering the river ecosystem as a complex and dynamic system of systems . With the purposive digital twin of the river at the core, we use a modeling and simulation (M&S)-based approach to comprehend emergent phenomena associated with river dynamics, explore interventions, and enable informed policy decisions in the face of inherent environmental uncertainty. A novel digital twin of the river ecosystem that combines agent- and physics-based models is presented. Agent-based modeling captures the systemic aspects of the river, including the behavioral patterns of various stakeholders and their dependencies at microlevel, while the physics-based models address the chemical composition dynamics and pollutant reactions under dynamic conditions at mesolevel. This hybrid approach enables the construction of a digital twin that simulates water quality parameters across diverse scenarios, including rainfall events, effluent discharges, demographic shifts, and climate change impacts for informed evidence-based decision-making. Title: Motion control of an aquatic snake robot with actuator failures and environmental uncertainties using neural network super twisting sliding mode control
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati, Assam, Guwahati, 781039, India; Advanced Research and Technology Office, MathWorks, Natick, 01760, MA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Patel B.M., Department of Mechanical Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati, Assam, Guwahati, 781039, India; Valenti R.G., Advanced Research and Technology Office, MathWorks, Natick, 01760, MA, United States; Dwivedy S.K., Department of Mechanical Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati, Assam, Guwahati, 781039, India
Abstract: Snake robots, designed to mimic the motion of biological snakes which can be used as versatile applications in underwater operations like maintenance and surveillance. In this work, the snake robot is designed and simulated in the Simscape multibody environment in which the need for explicit mathematical modelling is not required. Because of the multi-link construction, the robot features multiple actuators, raising the possibility of actuator failure. Understanding the robot’s motion in the event of such failures is crucial. Hence, this work examines different scenarios of actuator malfunction. Motion control is achieved through a virtual holonomic constraints (VHCs) based approach, considering various uncertainties in underwater environments. To deal with these uncertainties, the model-based robust control approach known as sliding mode control (SMC) is applied to a simplified dynamic system, which is formulated through virtual holonomic constraints (VHC). A radial basis function (RBF) neural network estimates the model, which is then integrated into the SMC control strategy. To mitigate the chattering issue associated with SMC, the super twisting sliding mode control (STSMC) strategy is employed. Consequently, we propose the RBF-STSMC scheme for controlling the motion of a snake robot in underwater conditions during single or multiple actuator failures and uncertain environments. This proposed scheme is evaluated against existing control strategies. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Multidimensional Cognitive-State Modeling and an Adaptive Cognitive Load Twin for AI-Supported Managerial Decision-Making
Affiliations: Management Information Systems, Atlas University, Istanbul, 34408, Turkey; Vocational School, Carbon Management Technicianship, Doğuş University, Istanbul, 34680, Turkey

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-supported decision systems can improve managerial decision-making, but their cognitive implications may depend on how information, explanations, alerts, time pressure, uncertainty, autonomy, and human control are configured. This study develops an Adaptive Cognitive Load Twin using data from 420 logistics and supply-chain professionals in Türkiye who completed four AI-supported managerial decision scenarios, yielding 1680 participant–scenario observations. The framework models information overload, cognitive load, decision fatigue, perceived explainability, trust in AI, automation bias, perceived human control, perceived decision quality, and objective decision accuracy as distinct but related dimensions. Participant-clustered path analysis showed that higher information overload was associated with higher cognitive load, and higher cognitive load was strongly associated with higher decision fatigue; in turn, higher cognitive load and decision fatigue were associated with lower perceived decision quality. Higher perceived explainability was associated with lower cognitive load, greater trust, higher perceived decision quality, and lower automation-bias tendency, while greater perceived human control was associated with higher perceived decision quality and lower automation bias. Higher cognitive load was associated with lower objective decision accuracy. Participant-grouped machine learning models showed that cognitive load was more predictable than decision fatigue or objective accuracy, with information density and time pressure emerging as leading predictive contributors. Model-based simulations indicated that lower information density and progressive disclosure offered the clearest opportunities for adaptive support. The framework extends digital-twin logic toward multidimensional, human-centered monitoring and adaptation of cognitive conditions in AI-assisted managerial work. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: A general closed-form second-moment framework for probabilistic updating of damped MDOF systems
Affiliations: James Watt School of Engineering, The University of Glasgow, Scotland, Glasgow, United Kingdom; Univ Lyon, Univ Gustave Eiffel, Univ Claude Bernard Lyon 1, LBMC UMR-T 9406, Lyon, F-69622, France
Authors with affiliations: Adhikari S., James Watt School of Engineering, The University of Glasgow, Scotland, Glasgow, United Kingdom; Jacquelin E., Univ Lyon, Univ Gustave Eiffel, Univ Claude Bernard Lyon 1, LBMC UMR-T 9406, Lyon, F-69622, France
Abstract: Probabilistic updating of damped structural systems lacks closed-form expressions for operator statistics, leaving iterative numerical methods or implicit auxiliary variable formulations that obscure analytical uncertainty propagation. This work develops a closed-form second-moment framework for simultaneous updating of mass, damping, and stiffness matrices under combined eigenvalue, eigenvector, and modal damping uncertainty, a combination for which explicit operator statistics were previously unavailable. The formulation exploits a sequential property of weighted Frobenius norm minimisation subject to modal orthogonality constraints, whereby the three updates are obtained in three successive convex steps. Stiffness updating depends only on measured frequencies, damping updating depends only on measured modal damping, and mass updating is deduced from the measured modal mass matrix through Berman’s incomplete-mode correction. Gaussian moment closures give exact mean operators, and Fréchet derivative-based perturbation expansions give Kronecker-structured sensitivity matrices that map modal uncertainty to physical-space operator covariance without auxiliary variables or nonlinear solvers. The cross-covariances between the identified modal quantities are retained throughout. Numerical verification on a non-proportionally damped benchmark confirms close analytical-Monte Carlo agreement for mean and covariance predictions, with cross-correlation inclusion yielding order-of-magnitude improvement over independence assumptions. The methodology exchanges finite-element sparsity for analytical tractability, positioning it as a component of digital twin applications, in which the updated operators are interpreted as reduced models condensed onto the instrumented degrees of freedom and the measured modes are taken to span that reduced space. In that setting operator-level uncertainty quantification supports probabilistic forward prediction, data assimilation, and lifecycle prognostics that sampling-based alternatives render prohibitive. The scope of the paper is the operator statistics themselves, and their embedding in a particular assimilation architecture is left open. The framework requires as many sensors as identified modes, with the analytical operators condensed onto those sensors, and it recovers the true mass exactly on the span of the identified modes. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Stockpile Reclamation and Grade Blending for Processing Plant Feed: A Systematic Review of Methods, Models, and Research Gaps
Affiliations: School of Mining and Petroleum Engineering, University of Alberta, Edmonton, T6G 1H9, AB, Canada; NTWIST Inc., Edmonton, T6N 1G1, AB, Canada
Authors with affiliations: Khazaei S., School of Mining and Petroleum Engineering, University of Alberta, Edmonton, T6G 1H9, AB, Canada; Noriega R., NTWIST Inc., Edmonton, T6N 1G1, AB, Canada; Askari-Nasab H., School of Mining and Petroleum Engineering, University of Alberta, Edmonton, T6G 1H9, AB, Canada; Pourrahimian Y., School of Mining and Petroleum Engineering, University of Alberta, Edmonton, T6G 1H9, AB, Canada
Abstract: Stockpiles and run-of-mine (ROM) pads are critical control points between mine production and processing plant feed. The grade, quality mix, and variability of material delivered to the crusher and mill are largely determined by how these structures are designed, built, and reclaimed. Despite the operational significance of stockpile management, the field remains fragmented across five distinct research streams—physical blending theory, stockpile state modelling, reclaim sequencing and equipment scheduling, plant-feed and stockpile blending optimization, and sensor-driven reconciliation and closed-loop control—with limited integration between them. This paper presents a systematic review of 27 sources published between 1976 and 2025, including peer-reviewed journal articles, conference papers, a preprint, a book, and one industry publication. The literature search was conducted in May 2025 using Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, with records screened by title/abstract and full text for direct relevance to stockpile reclamation or grade blending in mining operations. A structured coverage matrix identifies that studies combining high spatial fidelity with strong optimization rigor are consistently absent from the literature, and that uncertainty handling and sensor-driven or real-time capability remain substantially underdeveloped. Six research gaps are identified and prioritized by practical significance, implementation readiness, and literature maturity. The four most operationally critical gaps concern: spatially explicit reclaim scheduling under live ROM-pad constraints; tractable multi-attribute blending formulations for polymetallic operations; uncertainty propagation to plant-feed predictions; and field-scale closed-loop validation. The review provides a structured development roadmap for ROM-pad optimization frameworks and identifies the specific integration challenges that must be addressed to move the field from static stockpile monitoring toward adaptive, sensor-updated decision support. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: Hydrogen storage remains a central bottleneck for scalable hydrogen energy systems due to the multiscale and coupled nature of the thermodynamics, kinetics, and microstructural evolution of hydrogen storage materials (HSMs). Although artificial intelligence (AI) has accelerated materials discovery, current approaches remain constrained by fragmented data, limited physical consistency, and weak integration with experimental validation. Here, we propose a unified framework that integrates coherent data infrastructure, physics-grounded modeling, and AI-driven inverse design within a closed-loop discovery paradigm. By constraining optimization with thermodynamics, kinetics, uncertainty, provenance, and experimental feedback, this approach enables adaptive, physically consistent optimization, thereby establishing a pathway toward autonomous, digital-twin-enabled discovery of HSMs. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Geometric Imperfections in CFS Structures: A Comprehensive Review from Initial Measurement to Digital Design
Affiliations: School of Civil Engineering, Central South University, Changsha, 410075, China
Authors with affiliations: Shen Y., School of Civil Engineering, Central South University, Changsha, 410075, China; Zhang L., School of Civil Engineering, Central South University, Changsha, 410075, China; Cai Y., School of Civil Engineering, Central South University, Changsha, 410075, China
Abstract: Abstract: The nonlinear stability of cold-formed steel (CFS) members exhibits high sensitivity to initial geometric imperfections, which introduces uncertainties in the prediction of their ultimate load-bearing capacity. Although measurement technologies have evolved from point-based methods to full-field 3D scanning, current design codes still rely on simplified deterministic assumptions with low-fidelity data. This situation impedes the implementation of advanced analysis in design due to the lack of consensus on input parameters. This paper examines the disparity between the “high-precision measurement capabilities” and the “assimilation capacity of design methods” in the research on CFS geometric imperfections, and posits that bridging this gap necessitates a standardized probabilistic equivalent imperfection framework. Firstly, it assesses laser scanning and photogrammetry for capturing full-field geometric characteristics. Secondly, it tracks the evolution of modeling strategies from single eigenmode approaches to stochastic field models based on the spectral representation method (SRM) and Karhunen–Loève (K-L) expansion, highlighting data-driven methods for generating virtual specimens. Finally, it explores how high-fidelity models facilitate the transition from the implicit direct strength method (DSM) to explicit analysis-based design. In conclusion, the development of standardized probabilistic imperfection databases and their integration into digital twin frameworks are crucial for the next-generation precision prediction of CFS structures. © Pleiades Publishing, Ltd. 2026.

Title: Computational and Data-Driven Strategies for Lignocellulosic Biomass Valorization: From Multiscale Modeling to Digitalized Biorefinery Design

Abstract: Lignocellulosic biomass is a major renewable carbon resource for sustainable production of fuels, chemicals, and functional materials. Yet its valorization remains constrained by structural recalcitrance, feedstock heterogeneity, and the coupling of molecular and process phenomena. This review critically examines computational and data-driven strategies for predictive biorefinery development, with emphasis on how experimentally anchored information can be transferred across scales. Structural determinants of deconstructability, including cellulose organization, lignin chemistry, lignin-carbohydrate interactions, porosity, and accessibility, are assessed together with density functional theory, molecular dynamics, reactive simulations, thermodynamic and kinetic modeling, and machine learning. Particular attention is given to computational solvent design, catalytic upgrading, pyrolysis reaction networks, reactor-scale coupling, and the limitations imposed by model simplification, dataset heterogeneity, extrapolation, and uncertainty. Representative multiscale case studies illustrate validated information handoffs from detailed kinetics to CFD, molecular screening to experiment, and pretreatment to life-cycle assessment. FAIR data infrastructure, workflow automation, and digital twins are discussed as enabling layers. Future progress depends on experimentally validated scale transfer, multicycle durability of solvents and catalysts, uncertainty-aware modeling, and interoperable data ecosystems for practical biorefinery design. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: A probabilistic physics-based framework for the development and continuous adaptation of lifecycle digital twins
Affiliations: Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Institute for Computational and Mathematical Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; CMSoft, Inc., CA, United States; U.S. Air Force, United States
Authors with affiliations: Farhat C., Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Institute for Computational and Mathematical Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Daeninck G., CMSoft, Inc., CA, United States; Harp D.I., U.S. Air Force, United States
Abstract: Digital twins are increasingly employed to support predictive analysis, decision-making, and monitoring of complex physical systems. However, existing implementations often rely either on high-fidelity models that are computationally prohibitive for real-time operation or on purely data-driven surrogates that lack physical interpretability and robustness outside their training domain. We present a unified, physics-based computational framework for digital twinning that addresses these limitations through hierarchical projection-based model order reduction, nonparametric probabilistic representation of model-form uncertainty, and data-driven calibration and updating. The framework spans a hierarchy of reduced-order models, from high-dimensional models (HDMs) to hyperreduced stochastic surrogates, enabling computationally efficient predictions while preserving the essential physics of the underlying system. It establishes a systematic progression from an HDM to a digital twin prototype (DTP) through projection and hyperreduction, and subsequently to an operational digital twin instance (DTI) through asset-specific stochastic calibration. To achieve real-time predictive capability while capturing unsteady nonlinear behavior, the framework incorporates a novel trajectory-based perturbation formulation supported by a database of physical matrices acting as localized tangent operators of the underlying nonlinear equations. Interpretable and non-interpretable sources of model-form uncertainty are represented through low-dimensional stochastic parameterizations, enabling efficient uncertainty propagation, statistical inference, and continuous data-driven updating in reduced-order spaces. The framework is validated using two aerospace applications. The first demonstrates an operational DTP for an F-16D aircraft executing aggressive, unsteady maneuvers under the United States Air Force HAVE MIRAGE project, delivering physics-consistent online predictions from real flight data at 20 Hz (0.05 s intervals) in a faster-than-real-time setting – achieving speedup factors up to 57 × ahead of real-time on a single CPU. The second application demonstrates a DTI for structural health monitoring, inferring Level-1 damage presence through changes in the predictive consistency and confidence intervals of the digital twin, utilizing a synthetic dataset representing progressive degradation states. Within this structural tracking context, the hyperreduced stochastic forward solver yields a two-order-of-magnitude speedup factor of approximately 272 × over the HDM, enabling near-real-time tracking on a single standard core. Together, these applications demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a computationally efficient, physics-consistent foundation for digital twinning across the lifecycle of complex engineering systems. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Interpreting satellite radar for bridges: integrating MT-InSAR with physics-based and data-driven models for scalable structural health monitoring
Affiliations: Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Florida International University, Miami, 33174, FL, United States; Department of Civil Engineering, Kasetsart University, Bangkok, 10900, Thailand
Authors with affiliations: Khan A.Q., Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Florida International University, Miami, 33174, FL, United States; Pimanmas A., Department of Civil Engineering, Kasetsart University, Bangkok, 10900, Thailand
Abstract: Multi-Temporal Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (MT-InSAR) has matured into a credible, non-contact technique for monitoring bridge deformation from individual structures to regional portfolios. The main challenge for routine engineering use is no longer measuring millimetre-scale line-of-sight (LOS) displacement, but interpreting those measurements into defensible statements about structural condition. This review addresses that interpretation problem by synthesising the physical and algorithmic fundamentals of MT-InSAR, bridge-typology-dependent applicability, LOS projection ambiguity, current sensor capabilities, and emerging open data services. Particular emphasis is placed on signal decoupling because measured bridge displacement combines reversible thermal response, transient live-load effects, progressive deformation associated with damage or settlement, and measurement noise. Two complementary interpretation strategies are examined: physics-based integration using finite-element analysis, model updating and digital twins, and data-driven integration using clustering, anomaly detection, forecasting and deep learning. Their convergence through physics-informed methods is also discussed. The review proposes a hybrid framework in which data-driven methods screen bridge portfolios and identify anomalous deformation, while physics-based modelling provides structural interpretation and supports validation using inspection records, in-situ measurements and uncertainty quantification. The synthesis highlights the strengths and limitations of current practice and identifies research needs in multi-geometry analysis, dense spatial sampling, physics-informed learning, portfolio-scale digital twins and prospective validation. The resulting framework is intended to support scalable, physically interpretable and evidence-based use of MT-InSAR in bridge structural health monitoring. © The Author(s) 2026. Title: Digital Twins in Oncology: From Multimodal Data Integration to Precision Clinical Practice
Source title: Indian Journal of Radiology and Imaging
Affiliations: Madha Medical College and Research Institute, Tamil Nadu, Thandalam, India; Department of Medical Sciences and Technology, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras, Tamil Nadu, Chennai, India
Authors with affiliations: Vairavan A., Madha Medical College and Research Institute, Tamil Nadu, Thandalam, India; Bhattacharjee R., Department of Medical Sciences and Technology, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras, Tamil Nadu, Chennai, India; Raghavan B., Department of Medical Sciences and Technology, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras, Tamil Nadu, Chennai, India
Abstract: Oncology digital twins are patient-specific computational models that are built by combining electronic health records, multiomics genomic data, and diagnostic imaging to simulate individual tumor biology and predict multiple treatment-related outcomes. Conceptually originated from aerospace engineering, it has matured clinically through convergent advances in radiomics, mechanistic tumor modeling, pharmacokinetic- pharmacodynamic systems, federated machine learning, and, most recently, large language model (LLM)-based clinical interfaces and agentic artificial intelligence (AI). For a practicing radiologist, digital twins offer a transformative role: imaging-derived quantitative features serve as the primary data, positioning diagnostic imaging at the center of these personalized oncology workflows. Key clinical applications especially in oncology span from chemotherapy response prediction, immunotherapy patient selection, personalized radiation planning, tumor progression modeling, and treatment toxicity forecasting. Several of these applications are achievable with current technology without any significant infrastructure investment. Substantial challenges include imaging data standards, absence of prospective validation, algorithmic bias in underrepresented populations, and regulatory uncertainty for continuously self-updating AI. This narrative review provides radiologists with a balanced, comprehensive overview of digital twin architecture, advanced enabling technologies, current clinical evidence, a practical roadmap for implementation, and a candid appraisal of barriers to adoption. © 2026 Indian Radiological Association. Abstract: Ultrasonic Guided Wave (UGW)-based Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) is a promising strategy for detecting damage to aeronautical structures, although its application is complicated by signal complexity and experimental uncertainty. This work seeks to identify damage-sensitive signal features for integration into Machine Learning (ML) frameworks, offering physics-informed indicators. The study combined experimental monitoring of damage to Carbon Fibre Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) plates and finite element models. To overcome the numerical–experimental mismatch, an ML algorithm predicted experimental characteristics from numerical data. The robustness of the model was validated by extrapolation (prediction of future damage) and generalization (prediction on unseen plates) strategies, confirming that ML can robustly correct for uncertainty. These results validate hybrid strategies that feed Digital Twin approaches to structural diagnosis and real-time forecasting. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Uncertainty-aware future trajectory prediction and collision risk assessment for moving objects in manufacturing workspaces
Affiliations: Department of Applied Artificial Intelligence, Seoul National University of Science and Technology, Seoul, South Korea
Authors with affiliations: Hong M.J., Department of Applied Artificial Intelligence, Seoul National University of Science and Technology, Seoul, South Korea; Kim B.S., Department of Applied Artificial Intelligence, Seoul National University of Science and Technology, Seoul, South Korea
Abstract: This study proposes a deep learning framework for uncertainty-aware trajectory prediction and collision risk assessment in industrial environments. While uncertainty prediction methods exist, integrating them into an efficient, real-time industrial safety framework remains a challenge. Our framework addresses this gap by employing a Temporal Self-Attention Bi-LSTM model with Lower–Upper Bound Estimation (LUBE) to generate prediction intervals. Collision risk is then assessed using an Intersection over Union (IoU) metric on these intervals. To improve computational efficiency in multi-agent scenarios, the framework uses KNN-based candidate pairing, while a proximity-based dynamic IoU threshold provides adaptive risk sensitivity. Experiments on a Unity-based digital twin dataset validate our model's architecture through ablation studies. Furthermore, a real-world accident CCTV case study provides preliminary evidence of the framework’s feasibility for preemptive collision prediction. The results suggest the potential applicability of the framework for uncertainty-aware collision risk assessment in industrial environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Abstract: The study of meteors offers vital insights into the origin, evolution, and dynamics of celestial bodies within our solar system. The collection of meteor trajectories and identification of potential meteorite impact sites provides direct evidence of these astronomical phenomena. With meteors entering Earth’s atmosphere from random directions at unpredictable times, combined with the widespread availability of commercial cameras in surveillance networks, smartphones, and amateur astronomical equipment, the development of systematic data collection and analysis methods has become essential. This paper introduces the HuoLiuXing Project (meaning “Fireball Project” in Chinese), an integrated platform that combines artificial intelligence and digital twin for meteor data collection and management. The project implements multiple methodologies for observational data collection and employs convolutional neural networks for reliable meteor identification. To enhance scientific contributions, we establish digital twins of camera systems, complete with detailed installation and calibration protocols for various equipment types. These digital twins also account for measurement uncertainties and incorporate prior information into analyses. Additionally, we present the digital twin of the entire HuoLiuXing system, which calculates three-dimensional probability distributions of meteor trajectories and potential meteorite impact locations according to observation data from multiple cameras. Experimental validation confirms that our digital twin approach effectively and robustly estimates meteor trajectories and precisely determines possible meteorite landing sites. Since its deployment in 2022, the HuoLiuXing Project has collected over 1400 valid meteor reports from various cameras deployed across China.
