Title: Adaptive task planning based on physiological state estimation and state uncertainty improves performance in human–robot collaboration
Affiliations: Robotics Department, University of Michigan, 2505 Hayward Street, Ann Arbor, 48109, MI, United States; Robotics Department, Mechanical Engineering Department, University of Michigan, 2505 Hayward Street, Ann Arbor, 48109, MI, United States
Authors with affiliations: Rafter A., Robotics Department, University of Michigan, 2505 Hayward Street, Ann Arbor, 48109, MI, United States; Tilbury D.M., Robotics Department, Mechanical Engineering Department, University of Michigan, 2505 Hayward Street, Ann Arbor, 48109, MI, United States; Barton K., Robotics Department, Mechanical Engineering Department, University of Michigan, 2505 Hayward Street, Ann Arbor, 48109, MI, United States
Abstract: Human–robot collaboration combines the strengths of humans and robots to enhance productivity, flexibility, and safety. A task planner can use knowledge of relevant human and robot states to optimize overall task performance. Digital twins use models and real-time data to estimate these human and robot states. In our study, we implement a system of digital twins in which state information from a human–robot collaborative system is used to inform task reallocation in response to disruptions in team performance, with the goal of maximizing overall team throughput. The case study involves an assembly task in which three humans (one real, two simulated) work with a dual-arm robot. Humans are responsible for performing assembly operations, while the robot delivers parts. In aggregate, the digital twins predict the throughput of the human–robot collaborative system and detect disruptions, such as when the predicted throughput drops below a threshold. When a disruption is detected, the task planner reallocates tasks among agents based on their estimated capacity to maintain performance. The study examines how overall throughput is affected by varying levels of uncertainty in the predicted states of the human–robot collaborative system. In addition, the study explores how the task planner considers varying levels of human stress to allocate tasks and improve performance. The results of a study with 40 participants show that incorporating human stress estimates into task planning improves team performance, and that lower uncertainty values also improve team performance, but with a smaller effect. Together, these two factors improve throughput on average by 5.3% compared to a planner that uses high uncertainty and omits human stress estimates. These findings demonstrate that incorporating even simple physiological indicators and principled uncertainty filtering can significantly enhance task allocation decisions, offering a scalable approach to embedding human-aware intelligence into collaborative robotic systems. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Probabilistic Multimodal Digital Twins for Healthcare Monitoring
Source title: 2026 11th International Conference on Smart and Sustainable Technologies, SpliTech 2026
Affiliations: School of Information Technology, Halmstad University, Sweden; Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
Authors with affiliations: Sayeed S., School of Information Technology, Halmstad University, Sweden; Bavafa S., School of Information Technology, Halmstad University, Sweden; Roque A.D.S., School of Information Technology, Halmstad University, Sweden; De Freitas E.P., School of Information Technology, Halmstad University, Sweden, Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
Abstract: Probabilistic digital twins are increasingly explored for continuous and personalized healthcare monitoring in Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) environments. However, existing systems largely rely on fixed thresholds and deterministic rules that fail under noisy or incomplete data and contribute to alert fatigue. This paper presents a probabilistic digital twin framework that estimates latent ICU health states from physiological signals through a Bayesian Hidden Markov Model, with a behavioral modality integrated as an architectural extension demonstrated on a cross-dataset cohort, maintaining an online belief state for continuous, uncertainty-aware health status estimation. Evaluated on 64,691 intensive care unit (ICU) patients from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) dataset across 9,890,935 observation windows, the framework achieves an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.687, competitive with a supervised logistic regression baseline (AUC=0.740), with a median lead-time of 12.0 hours before vasopressor onset and 3.13 days before in-hospital death. Age-adjusted belief-state initialization personalizes risk estimation per patient, while a glass-box changebased attribution layer provides per-window clinical explanations without post-hoc approximation. A parameter sweep identifies conservative state transitions as the optimal operating point, maintaining a 14.7% false alarm rate. The framework offers a probabilistic and explainable monitoring approach suitable for Healthcare 5.0 applications. © 2026 University of Split, FESB.

Title: Enabling Resilient Retail Warehousing: Managerial Strategies for Mitigating Supply Chain Disruptions
Affiliations: Medline Industries, LP, Northfield, IL, United States; Genuine Parts Company, Atlanta, GA, United States; Undocked Inc, Alpharetta, GA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Thiyagarajan S., Medline Industries, LP, Northfield, IL, United States; Perumal P.J., Genuine Parts Company, Atlanta, GA, United States; Kulkarni A., Undocked Inc, Alpharetta, GA, United States
Abstract: Retail warehousing stability is increasingly threatened by global supply chain volatility, unpredictable demand shocks, labor shortages, and rising operational complexity. Persistent disruptions expose structural vulnerabilities in traditional warehouse management approaches, underscoring the critical need for more adaptive, technology-enabled, and human-centered strategies. This qualitative pragmatic inquiry examined how retail warehousing managers mitigate disruption impacts to preserve operational stability, stakeholder trust, and customer satisfaction. Grounded in situational crisis communication theory and attribution theory, the study explored managers’ communication choices and response behaviors during operational and supply chain crises. Six operational managers from retail warehousing facilities contributed insights through semi-structured interviews. Thematic analysis revealed four central themes: (1) adaptability and organizational resilience core capabilities for continuity under uncertainty; (2) proactive crisis planning and transparent communication as mechanisms for maintaining stakeholder confidence; (3) workforce optimization strategies including cross-training, flexible scheduling, and rapid redeployment; and (4) reliance on data-driven performance metrics to guide real-time decisions and continuous improvement. Findings further highlight the growing role of predictive analytics, AI-enabled forecasting, real-time monitoring systems, and digital twin applications in anticipating disruptions, optimizing labor allocation, and mitigating bottlenecks. Recommendations encourage retail warehousing leaders to adopt integrated human-technology strategies that improve agility, strengthen crisis communication, and embed metric-informed interventions. Practical implications include improved business continuity, enhanced service-level performance, and greater frontline job stability. This study contributes actionable insights for industry practitioners and advances pathways for positive social change by equipping managers to sustain operations and safeguard workforce livelihoods in increasingly volatile supply chains. © (2026) by Institute of Industrial & Systems Engineers (IISE) All rights reserved.
